dateReview.note: 690–705 is Wu Zetian’s imperial Zhou period, as distinguished from her earlier dominance of the Tang court.

cards.significance: Wu Zetian (武则天)'s reign made the basis of imperial authority unusually visible. A woman claiming the emperor's title needed officials, religious support and persuasive accounts of her legitimacy in a political order usually organized around male succession. Her promotion of writers and examination candidates also connected cultural achievement to access to power. The importance lies in how she exercised and defended authority, as well as her exceptional position. Tang's restoration did not erase the careers and institutions developed during her rule.

significanceSources.label: Xiaofei Tian · Poetry and Access to Power

image.alt: An inscribed limestone epitaph displayed on a wall.
image.caption: The 693 epitaph of Yang Shun, a general under Wu Zhao, in the Royal Ontario Museum. An inscription provides contemporary evidence for office and commemoration under her Zhou dynasty.

cards.name: Five Dynasties
cards.description: Between Tang’s fall in 907 and Song’s foundation in 960, five dynasties succeeded one another in the north. Some regional states lasted much longer. Military commanders could make and unmake emperors, but government did not start again from nothing with each new ruling family.
cards.note: 907–960 concerns the five northern dynasties. The wider regional division extends beyond those dates.
cards.catalogNote: 907–960 is supported; Sui–Tang is an editorial aggregate, not one dynasty.

sections.title: Armies and personal loyalty
sections.text: Commanders depended on relationships with their troops and on access to money and supplies. These ties could help a ruler take power, then allow another commander to overthrow him. Offices, armies and regional centres often survived a change of dynasty, even when the people at the top changed quickly.

sections.title: The foundations of Song
sections.text: Later Zhou strengthened its military and government and expanded its territory before Song was founded. Song inherited that work and continued the struggle to bring regional states under one court. The year 960 therefore marks a new dynasty, not an instant end to division. Reunification depended on campaigns and negotiations that continued after the Five Dynasties period.

sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs: Naomi Standen · Five Dynasties
sourceLabels.https://assets.cambridge.org/97811070/84: Peter Lorge · The Reunification of China: excerpt
sourceLabels.https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.7312/dav: Ouyang Xiu / Richard Davis · Historical Records of the Five Dynasties

dateReview.note: 907–960 is supported; Sui–Tang is an editorial aggregate, not one dynasty.

cards.significance: This period helps explain why the Song court worried so much about controlling its own commanders. Repeated military takeovers had shown that the army defending an emperor could also replace him. Yet the road to Song was built through these governments: armies, revenue systems and territorial gains survived changes at the top. The period connects Tang's regional military power to Song's efforts at consolidation. Treating it only as chaos hides the institutions that made a more durable dynasty possible.

significanceSources.label: Naomi Standen · Five Dynasties
Peter Lorge · The Reunification of China: excerpt

image.credit: Artist or photographer unidentified · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: Women gathered inside a palace in a vertical painting.
image.caption: Palace Banquet, a painting assigned to the tenth-century Five Dynasties–early Song milieu, in the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Court culture continued across rapid political changes.

cards.name: Song
cards.description: Founded in 960, Song brought much of the former Tang heartland under one court while sharing East Asia with powerful neighbouring empires. Growing markets, printed books and examinations helped shape its society. Trade and learning flourished alongside the continuing demands of war.
cards.note: 960–1279. Northern Song ends in 1127; Southern Song continues to 1279. Regional prosperity and political boundaries changed substantially within both periods.

sections.title: Markets and education
sections.text: Specialized producers supplied towns and cities through expanding markets. Printing made study texts more available, while examinations offered educated families a route into government. These developments created opportunities, but preparation still required time, teachers and money. Commercial growth also left families exposed to debt, failed harvests and taxes.

sections.title: Survival in the south
sections.text: Jin forces took the northern capital in 1127, but the Song ruling house rebuilt its government in the south. Southern farming, cities and transport routes supplied the money and grain needed to maintain armies. The dynasty continued until 1279, resisting first Jin and then the Mongols. Wealth gave it resources to fight; turning those resources into lasting security remained a difficult political and military task.

dateReview.note: 960–1279 is secure; the 1127 division and incomplete territorial unification are correctly noted.

cards.significance: Song connects imperial history to changes in everyday opportunity: expanding markets, printed learning and examinations brought commerce and education into the ambitions of more families. These developments continued even when the dynasty lost the north. They help explain the lasting importance of southern cities and of the educated official in later Chinese society. Song also shows why wealth and security must be studied separately. Commercial resources sustained resistance for generations, but turning money into reliable defence required difficult military and political choices.

significanceSources.label: Columbia University · Song society

image.alt: A seated emperor in red court robes.
image.caption: A court portrait of Song Taizu, Zhao Kuangyin. Imperial portraiture asserts dynastic authority; the image is not a literal record of the military transfer of power in 960.

cards.name: Yuan
cards.description: Kublai Khan (忽必烈) proclaimed the Yuan dynasty in 1271 and completed the conquest of Southern Song in 1279. His government connected China to Mongol networks across Eurasia. People of many backgrounds worked for the court, though their rights, duties and opportunities differed.
cards.note: 1271 marks the Yuan proclamation; 1279 marks the final conquest of Southern Song. Northern Yuan rule continued after 1368.
cards.catalogNote: 1271 dates the Yuan dynastic name, 1279 the final Song conquest. 1368 ends Yuan rule from Beijing, not all subsequent Mongol or Northern Yuan rule.

sections.title: Movement and unequal opportunity
sections.text: Officials, artisans and religious specialists travelled to serve rulers and patrons. Some found employment and protection; others moved because of conquest, displacement or forced service. The court’s cultural variety grew through both opportunity and coercion. Connections across great distances did not mean that everyone in the empire enjoyed equal standing.

sections.title: China and the Mongol world
sections.text: Yuan rulers used Chinese forms of government while keeping close political ties to Mongolia and the steppe. Their claims to wider Mongol authority did not make every other Mongol khanate obey them. When Ming forces took Dadu (大都) in 1368, Yuan rule over the Chinese heartland ended. Its rulers and their successors continued to govern farther north.

dateReview.note: 1271 dates the Yuan dynastic name, 1279 the final Song conquest. 1368 ends Yuan rule from Beijing, not all subsequent Mongol or Northern Yuan rule.

cards.significance: Yuan brought northern and southern China under one dynasty while placing their government inside a wider Mongol political world. This redirected the movement of administrators, craftspeople, religious specialists and knowledge across Eurasia. Those connections helped shape later Chinese material culture and institutions, but conquest and unequal privileges determined who benefited. Yuan belongs within Chinese dynastic history and within the history of Mongol expansion at the same time. Keeping both perspectives explains changes that a simple story of foreign interruption would miss.

significanceSources.label: Columbia University · Mongols in China

image.alt: A painted portrait of Kublai Khan in a white robe and fur-trimmed hat.
image.caption: Kublai Khan’s portrait from the Yuan imperial album, traditionally associated with Araniko. It represents the ruler through court portraiture, rather than illustrating a specific proclamation.

cards.name: Ming
cards.description: Zhu Yuanzhang (朱元璋) rose through rebellions against the Yuan and founded the Ming dynasty in 1368. His court rebuilt imperial government and presented its rule as a restoration of good order. Over the next three centuries, growing cities, trade and publishing changed the society it governed.
cards.note: 1368–1644 describes the main Ming court. Southern Ming claimants continued after Beijing (北京) fell; the existing 1662 endpoint is explained on their separate card.
cards.catalogNote: 1368–1644 is the main Ming court convention. Southern Ming successors survived after Beijing fell.

sections.title: Building a new dynasty
sections.text: The Ming drew on earlier institutions and traditions to establish its authority. Court ceremonies, scholarship and painting helped present the new rulers as rightful emperors. Artists revived older styles, while officials adapted older ways of governing to new circumstances. These choices connected the dynasty to a respected past and gave a former rebel a language in which to claim the throne.

sections.title: A growing commercial world
sections.text: In the later Ming, readers bought more books and wealthy households bought more luxury goods. Silver linked taxes and trade to distant markets. These changes created opportunities, but people also faced changing prices and heavy obligations. Rebellion, financial strain and war converged in the dynasty’s final years. After Beijing (北京) fell in 1644, Ming loyalist courts continued in the south.

dateReview.note: 1368–1644 is the main Ming court convention. Southern Ming successors survived after Beijing fell.

cards.significance: The Ming helped establish the institutions and cultural forms that its Qing successors would inherit. Its rulers claimed authority by restoring respected traditions, while artists and merchants adapted those traditions to changing tastes and expanding markets. This combination matters: a dynasty could celebrate an ancient ideal while governing a society that was changing around it. The Ming therefore connects the older imperial order with the commercial and cultural world of the last centuries of imperial China.

significanceSources.label: Cambridge History of China · Ming government
Metropolitan Museum · Ming dynasty

image.alt: A seated emperor in yellow robes before a decorated throne.
image.caption: A formal portrait of the Hongwu emperor, founder of the Ming. Dynastic portraiture represents authority; it is not a depiction of the rebellion or conquest that produced it.

cards.name: Qing
cards.description: The Qing dynasty began in the northeast in 1636. Its armies took Beijing (北京) in 1644 and made the former Ming capital their own. The conquest continued for decades, as Ming loyalists resisted in the south. Qing rule eventually lasted until the emperor’s abdication in 1912.
cards.note: 1636: dynastic foundation. 1644: Beijing (北京) conquest and start of rule from the Ming capital. 1912: imperial abdication; the revolutionary outbreak was in 1911.
cards.catalogNote: 1644–1912 is valid for rule from Beijing. The Qing dynastic name was proclaimed in 1636; the emperor abdicated on 12 February 1912, after the revolution began in 1911.

sections.title: Governing a diverse empire
sections.text: The Manchu ruling house used Chinese imperial offices and ceremonies while preserving its own military institutions. It also worked with Mongol and Tibetan leaders and supported Buddhist institutions. Different regions had different relationships with the court. The emperor’s authority therefore depended on several traditions of rule, alongside the officials who collected taxes and managed local government.

sections.title: Expansion and crisis
sections.text: The empire grew in territory and population. Trade supported prosperous regions, but feeding people, raising money and maintaining order placed growing demands on government. During the nineteenth century, devastating civil wars and attacks by foreign powers strained these arrangements. Officials tried new military and industrial projects as they struggled to preserve the dynasty. Its long history includes expansion and prosperity as well as its troubled final decades.

sourceLabels.https://afe.easia.columbia.edu/qing/empe: Columbia University · Qing emperors and a multiethnic empire

dateReview.note: 1636–1912 is correct for proclamation through abdication; the chart interval 1644–1912 properly distinguishes the Beijing phase.

cards.significance: The Qing left later governments a central problem: how to turn a large, diverse imperial realm into a modern nation. Its rulers governed different peoples through different institutions rather than making every region identical. After the monarchy fell, republicans had to decide which territories, communities and obligations the new state would inherit. Understanding that legacy helps explain why modern Chinese history involves arguments about territory and belonging as well as changes of government. Imperial boundaries and present borders should not be treated as interchangeable.

significanceSources.label: Columbia University · Qing rulers and the multiethnic empire

image.credit: J.H. Stewart Lockhart（骆克） · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: A printed illustration of both sides of a coin with Manchu writing.
image.caption: An 1895 numismatic illustration of a coin associated with Hong Taiji. The object’s Manchu inscription recalls Qing state formation before the conquest of Beijing; the illustration itself is much later.

cards.name: Republic of China (mainland period)
cards.description: The Republic of China was founded on 1 January 1912. The Qing emperor abdicated on 12 February, ending the dynasty. The new republic faced competing armies, political divisions, war with Japan and civil war. In 1949 its government relocated to Taiwan (台湾), where it continued.
cards.note: This card covers the Republic of China’s mainland period, 1912–1949. Its government relocated to Taiwan (台湾) in 1949 and continued there; the separate Taiwan (台湾) card covers that history.
cards.catalogNote: 1 January 1912 is the republic’s founding. 1949 ends this mainland-period card, not the existence of the ROC government, which relocated to Taiwan. Qing abdication followed on 12 February 1912.

sections.title: Who would govern the republic?
sections.text: Ending the monarchy left difficult questions. A parliament could pass laws, but military leaders controlled armies and much of the country’s resources. Rival governments and regional commanders competed for power. The Nationalists later tried to bring the country under their government through new institutions and military force. Political coercion accompanied the effort to establish national authority.

sections.title: War and a divided future
sections.text: War with Japan placed enormous demands on civilians and armies. Civil war then brought Communist victory on the mainland and the Republic’s relocation to Taiwan (台湾). This card covers the mainland period, 1912–1949. The Republic’s government continued beyond that boundary. Its later history in Taiwan (台湾) includes authoritarian rule and a gradual transition to democracy, covered in the separate Taiwan (台湾) entry.

sourceLabels.https://history.state.gov/countries/chin: U.S. Office of the Historian · Recognition and diplomatic relations
sourceLabels.https://1997-2001.state.gov/background_n: U.S. State Department · Taiwan historical background (2000)

dateReview.note: 1 January 1912 is the republic’s founding. 1949 ends this mainland-period card, not the existence of the ROC government, which relocated to Taiwan. Qing abdication followed on 12 February 1912.

cards.significance: The republic changed the stated source of political authority from a ruling family to a nation of citizens. Making that principle work proved much harder than announcing it: rival armies, unequal foreign privileges and war repeatedly weakened national institutions. The period matters because both Nationalists and Communists developed their organizations and competing answers to these problems within it. The division of 1949 emerged from this struggle; it was not already determined when the republic was founded.

significanceSources.label: U.S. Office of the Historian · Chinese Revolution of 1911
U.S. Office of the Historian · Chinese Revolution of 1949

image.alt: Sun Yat-sen and Li Yuanhong standing together in formal dress.
image.caption: Sun Yat-sen and Li Yuanhong at Wuchang in April 1912. Their encounter belongs to the early republic’s effort to convert revolutionary coalitions into a functioning state.

cards.name: People’s Republic of China
cards.description: Mao Zedong (毛泽东) proclaimed the People’s Republic of China on 1 October 1949 after Communist victories on the mainland. The Communist Party set out to redistribute land, expand industry and reorganize society. Later economic reforms brought major changes while the party retained control of national political power.
cards.note: 1949 dates the proclamation, not the end of all fighting or the completion of territorial consolidation. The endpoint is the exhibition horizon.
cards.catalogNote: Proclaimed 1 October 1949. 2026 is the dataset display horizon, not an end date.

sections.title: Revolution reaches everyday life
sections.text: The new government extended its authority through local party organizations, political campaigns, workplaces and economic planning. Land redistribution and expanded basic services changed many lives. Coercion and disastrous policies also caused immense suffering. The Great Leap Forward brought a devastating famine, and the Cultural Revolution disrupted education, families and government. These campaigns had different aims and consequences.

sections.title: A different economic direction
sections.text: From the late 1970s, reforms changed farming, business and connections with overseas markets. Families, factories and cities encountered new opportunities and pressures. The state’s name remained the same through these sharp changes in policy. The individual entries explain those turning points, including reform and opening, special economic zones and China’s entry into the World Trade Organization.

sourceLabels.https://history.state.gov/milestones/194: U.S. Office of the Historian · Chinese Revolution of 1949
sourceLabels.https://afe.easia.columbia.edu/special/c: Columbia · Leaders of the People’s Republic
sourceLabels.https://blogs.worldbank.org/en/eastasiap: World Bank · Forty years of reforms

dateReview.note: Proclaimed 1 October 1949. 2026 is the dataset display horizon, not an end date.

cards.significance: The founding of the People’s Republic brought a party committed to social revolution into control of the mainland. Government now reached deeply into landholding, workplaces, education and family life. Later reforms changed many economic arrangements without ending Communist Party rule. This makes the period essential for understanding how China could move from collective farming and central planning toward extensive market activity under the same ruling party. The gains, coercion and policy disasters belong to that shared history, rather than separate stories of uninterrupted progress or decline.

significanceSources.label: Columbia University · Leaders of the People’s Republic
World Bank · Forty years of China’s reforms

cards.pinyin: zhōng huá rén mín gòng hé guó

image.alt: Mao Zedong speaking at a row of microphones above a crowd.
image.caption: Mao Zedong proclaiming the People’s Republic of China on 1 October 1949. The ceremony established a public claim to state authority while military and political consolidation continued.

cards.name: Three Kingdoms
cards.description: Wei, Shu and Wu emerged as Han power collapsed. Each court claimed a right to inherit or continue imperial rule, but their territories and resources were unequal. Their formal division followed decades of fighting; it did not suddenly begin in 220.
cards.catalogNote: 220–280 follows the museum chronology.

sections.title: Three rival courts
sections.text: All three used people and methods inherited from Han. Shu claimed to restore Han, while Wei received the imperial title through a transfer from the last Han emperor. Wu established its own southern court. These were rival governments competing over an imperial inheritance, rather than three permanent national identities.

sections.title: What an army could sustain
sections.text: Commanders needed food, transport and enough people to keep campaigning. Rivers, farming settlements and cooperation with local powerful families helped determine where armies could go and how long they could stay. Later stories celebrate clever plans and memorable heroes. Those plans still faced material limits: even a talented commander could not feed soldiers or replace exhausted resources through ingenuity alone.

sourceLabels.https://www.chinaknowledge.de/History/Di: Ulrich Theobald · Three Kingdoms political history
Ulrich Theobald · Three Kingdoms military organization

cards.note: 220–280 is the conventional dynastic frame. Wu’s imperial proclamation came in 229, although its separate kingship is often dated 222.

dateReview.note: 220–280 follows the museum chronology.

cards.significance: The Three Kingdoms show how the ideal of one empire could survive while no court could achieve it. Each government drew on Han practices, but regional resources and alliances made separate centres of power durable. Their rivalry helped establish the political importance of Sichuan (四川) and the lower Yangtze (长江) alongside the north. Later storytelling gave these struggles an extraordinary cultural afterlife. For understanding the larger history, the central issue is how a shared imperial inheritance supported competing claims rather than automatically producing unity.

significanceSources.label: ChinaKnowledge · Three Kingdoms political history
ChinaKnowledge · Three Kingdoms military history

image.credit: Auckland War Memorial Museum Tāmaki Paenga Hira · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: A dark clay model of a saddled horse.
image.caption: An unglazed pottery horse attributed to the Wei dynasty, in Auckland Museum. A funerary object offers material evidence alongside the dynastic chronicles.

cards.name: Jin
cards.description: The Sima family’s Jin dynasty reunited the main successor states in 280. Fighting within the ruling family and upheaval in the north soon broke that unity. A Jin court survived in the south until 420, so the dynasty lasted much longer than its period of broad control.
cards.note: 266–420 includes Western and Eastern Jin; reunification in 280 did not last throughout the dynasty.

sections.title: Princes with armies
sections.text: Giving imperial relatives troops and regional authority could help protect the ruling family. It also gave rival princes resources to fight one another when succession became disputed. Winning territory had not settled how power would pass between rulers or who would command the armies. Family protection became a source of destructive conflict.

sections.title: Starting again in the south
sections.text: The southern court kept the Jin name, but depended on families who had moved south and powerful people already living there. It had to build new agreements to govern. The names Western Jin and Eastern Jin describe this major change in territory and support, as well as a move of the court. The later dynasty could not simply recreate the world it had lost.

sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/cam: Cambridge History of China · Western Jin
sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs: Cambridge History of China · Eastern Jin

dateReview.note: 266–420 is the combined Western and Eastern Jin span. Foundation can appear as 265 under another calendrical convention.

cards.significance: Jin demonstrates the distance between winning an empire and keeping its rulers, armies and leading families working together. Its brief reunification did not solve the conflicts within the governing elite. The dynasty’s survival in the south then helped carry an imperial claim and northern cultural resources into a different regional society. That movement matters beyond Jin itself: the southern courts that followed grew in a world reshaped by these migrations and political bargains, not simply in a smaller copy of the old northern empire.

significanceSources.label: Cambridge History of China · Eastern Jin

image.credit: Gary Todd from Xinzheng, China · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: A pale glazed figurine of a woman wearing a long robe.
image.caption: A Western Jin porcelain figure. The burial object provides a view of elite representation during the dynasty that briefly reunited the Three Kingdoms.

cards.name: Sixteen Kingdoms
cards.description: The Sixteen Kingdoms were competing northern states of the fourth and early fifth centuries. Their rulers drew on mixed armies and shifting alliances within the former Jin realm. Older accounts use the derogatory label “Five Barbarians” for Xiongnu, Jie, Xianbei, Di and Qiang groups. These were not five united peoples carrying out one invasion.
cards.catalogNote: 304–439 follows the museum chronology.

sections.title: How rulers built support
sections.text: Founders from different communities adopted imperial titles, recruited officials and governed mixed populations. Their family origins alone cannot explain how their states worked. Alliances among commanders, inherited methods of government and support for religious communities helped rulers gather authority. Loyalties could shift as courts rose and fell.

sections.title: Why sixteen?
sections.text: Later historians selected sixteen regimes to organize a much more crowded history. The name does not mean sixteen governments all existed at once, and other significant states can also be counted. Looking at individual courts reveals different choices about governing and survival. The period included more than warfare: officials and communities continued building institutions even while rulers competed.

cards.note: 304–439 is a conventional framework. More than sixteen significant regimes can be identified depending on the criteria.

dateReview.note: 304–439 follows the museum chronology.

cards.significance: These northern states make it impossible to reduce Chinese history to a single ruling population passing power down a straight line. Leaders with different family origins governed mixed communities and competed through familiar imperial titles as well as military force. Their courts could be short-lived while their religious and administrative connections lasted longer. Northern Wei’s later consolidation grew from this crowded political landscape. Following the individual states shows how new imperial societies formed through conflict, accommodation and movement across communities.

significanceSources.label: Cambridge History of China · The Sixteen Kingdoms

image.alt: A small gilded bronze Buddha seated with hands held before the body.
image.caption: A gilded bronze Buddha dated 338, made under Later Zhao and now in the Asian Art Museum, San Francisco. Its inscription anchors Buddhist patronage within the northern regimes.

cards.name: Northern and Southern Dynasties
cards.description: From 420, successive southern dynasties ruled alongside courts in the north. Both regions developed centres of government and culture. Migration, diplomacy and war connected them, even while rulers competed for territory and the right to govern.
cards.note: 420–589 marks the conventional Southern and Northern Dynasties frame. Northern Wei began earlier, in 386.
cards.catalogNote: 420–589 is a supported periodization; Northern Wei began earlier, in 386. Do not infer containment of all northern states.

sections.title: The southern courts
sections.text: Courts at Jiankang (建康) relied on military commanders, powerful families and the resources of the Yangtze (长江) region. Their history includes struggles at home as well as efforts to conquer the north. Their government and culture developed under these local conditions. Measuring them only by whether they reunited China would miss much of what people built and contested in the south.

sections.title: Experiments in northern government
sections.text: Northern rulers tried different ways to register households, distribute land and organize troops. They also supported religious communities. Some of these practices influenced later dynasties, but no single plan directed them toward Sui reunification. Different courts were trying to solve the immediate problem of ruling diverse populations after earlier empires had broken apart.

sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs: Cambridge History of China · Southern dynasties
Albert Dien · Western Wei and Northern Zhou

dateReview.note: 420–589 is a supported periodization; Northern Wei began earlier, in 386. Do not infer containment of all northern states.

cards.significance: Northern and southern courts developed different strengths that later rulers had to bring together. The north contributed powerful military networks and experiments in land administration; the south sustained major centres of learning, court culture and regional government. Neither side was culturally sealed off from the other. Their eventual political union required adapting these inheritances, not erasing centuries of change. This period therefore helps explain why Sui and Tang institutions combined experience drawn from several rival dynasties and regions.

significanceSources.label: Metropolitan Museum of Art · China, 500–1000
ChinaKnowledge · Northern Dynasties

image.alt: Rows of painted terracotta soldiers in a museum.
image.caption: Northern Wei funerary figures from the tomb of Sima Jinlong, dated 484. Their dress and organization offer evidence for elite military identity in the north.

cards.name: Liao
cards.description: The Khitan-led Liao empire governed pastoral communities and farming regions north of Song. Its rulers claimed to be emperors in their own right. Liao helped shape the borders, diplomacy and trade of the region for more than two centuries.
cards.note: 916 marks the imperial proclamation. Some chronologies begin in 907, when Abaoji (阿保机) became leader. Western Liao continued after 1125.
cards.catalogNote: 907–1125 is a supported Khitan-state convention; 916 denotes imperial proclamation. Name already qualifies Liao as Khitan.

sections.title: Different ways of governing
sections.text: The court used different arrangements for different populations and tasks. Mobile court practices existed alongside Chinese-style administration in farming regions. This allowed rulers to draw on several kinds of resources and expertise. It also meant managing competing powerful families and deciding who owed military service and who held office.

sections.title: Peace with Song
sections.text: The agreement of 1005 established mutual recognition and annual transfers from Song. Payments could be controversial, but they offered an alternative to the costs and destruction of repeated war. Jurchen forces conquered Liao’s heartland in 1125. Khitan survivors carried their power west, where Western Liao continued. The fall of the original court did not end Khitan political history.

sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/: Paul Jakov Smith · The fragility of the Chanyuan peace

dateReview.note: 916 is the formal imperial-state milestone; 907 dates Abaoji’s earlier accession and is used by the source dataset. Retain 916 with this distinction.

cards.significance: Liao makes clear that the history of this period cannot be told through the Song court alone. Its rulers governed farming and pastoral populations through different arrangements, demonstrating how an empire could draw strength from more than one political tradition. Its military and diplomatic power helped make negotiated coexistence a practical necessity for Song. The result was a regional order with several centres of authority, not one court whose claims automatically described what every neighbouring population experienced.

significanceSources.label: University of Washington · Khitan history

image.alt: An elaborate gold-coloured crown with pierced ornament.
image.caption: A gilt-silver Khitan crown from the tomb of the Princess of Chen State and her husband, early eleventh century. The object makes Liao elite ceremonial culture visible.

cards.name: Western Xia
cards.description: Li Yuanhao (李元昊) proclaimed Western Xia in 1038, building on an older Tangut power base in the northwest. Its territory connected farming districts, the steppe and the Hexi (河西) corridor. These routes made it a trading partner and military rival of neighbouring states.
cards.catalogNote: 1038 dates imperial proclamation by Li Yuanhao; Tangut power predates it. UNESCO's reviewed chronology supports 1038–1227.

sections.title: Books in Tangut
sections.text: The Tangut script gave the government a written language for administration and supported a rich Buddhist culture. Translators, scribes and printers produced works that connected the court to wider religious traditions. Surviving books reveal an important centre of learning, although Buddhist and archaeological evidence tells us more about some parts of society than others.

sections.title: Living between powerful neighbours
sections.text: Western Xia fought and negotiated with Song, Liao and Jin. Payments and recognition could secure breathing room without ending the Tangut court’s ability to govern its own territory. These changing relationships helped sustain the state for nearly two centuries. Mongol conquest ended it in 1227, after a long history of Tangut participation in the region’s balance of power.

cards.note: 1038 marks imperial proclamation, not the beginning of Tangut rule in the region. The surviving evidence is disproportionately Buddhist and archaeological.

sourceLabels.https://brill.com/display/book/978900446: Brill · Introduction to the Western Xia historical record

dateReview.note: 1038 dates imperial proclamation by Li Yuanhao; Tangut power predates it. UNESCO's reviewed chronology supports 1038–1227.

cards.significance: Western Xia gave the northwest an enduring centre of political and religious life between larger powers. Its command of routes and its ability to negotiate helped it survive without conquering the entire region. Tangut writing and Buddhist books show that this was also a society producing its own knowledge and institutions. Its importance broadens the map of Chinese history: the northwest was an active participant in shaping trade, diplomacy and belief, rather than simply territory contested by other dynasties.

significanceSources.label: UNESCO World Heritage Centre

image.credit: Gary Todd from Xinzheng, China · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: A painted Daoist deity seated within an ornamental composition.
image.caption: A Western Xia silk painting of the Daoist deity Xuanwu from the Hongfo Pagoda. The object complicates the assumption that the Tangut state’s religious life was exclusively Buddhist.

cards.name: Jin (Jurchen)
cards.description: Aguda (阿骨打) founded the Jurchen Jin dynasty in 1115. Its armies defeated Liao and captured the Song capital in 1127. Jin then governed much of northern China while Southern Song continued beyond a contested frontier.
cards.catalogNote: 1115–1234 dates the Jurchen Jin; distinct from the earlier Jin (晋).

sections.title: From conquest to government
sections.text: Jin rulers kept Jurchen military and social institutions while using Chinese administrative practices to govern farming communities. Questions of land, service and official appointments shaped how these arrangements worked together. Adopting a form of government did not automatically erase differences between conquerors and conquered, or the privileges associated with them.

sections.title: Life in the north
sections.text: People under Jin rule cultivated land, maintained towns and adapted to war and changes of government. Their history continued alongside the better-known cultural life of Southern Song. Mongol attacks brought another major upheaval, ending the dynasty in 1234. Song helped fight its northern rival, but Jin’s destruction left Song facing the expanding Mongol power.

cards.note: 1115–1234. This is the Jurchen Jin, 金, distinct from the earlier Jin dynasty, 晋, of 266–420.

dateReview.note: 1115–1234 dates the Jurchen Jin; distinct from the earlier Jin (晋).

cards.significance: Jin's conquests reshaped the political map and made the division between a northern empire and Southern Song a lasting reality. Northern farming communities, cities and cultural life continued under Jurchen rulers, so following Song south tells only part of China's history. Jin also stands between two major changes in regional power: its defeat of Liao and its own defeat by the Mongols. Song's participation in those struggles shows how removing a rival could expose a dynasty to a more dangerous neighbour.

significanceSources.label: The Metropolitan Museum of Art

image.credit: Scott Semans World Coins (CoinCoin.com) · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: Several bronze cash coins with square holes and Chinese inscriptions.
image.caption: Zhenglong yuanbao coins of the Jurchen Jin, dated 1158–1161. Chinese-script cash belonged to the governing practices of a dynasty founded by Jurchen rulers.

cards.name: Yuan foundation
cards.description: Kublai Khan (忽必烈) proclaimed the Yuan dynasty in 1271, eight years before the final defeat of Southern Song. He already ruled northern China and claimed authority as Great Khan. Southern Song still controlled territory that his new dynasty claimed.

sections.title: What the new name meant
sections.text: A Chinese dynastic title presented Kublai’s rule as part of an established tradition of imperial succession. It addressed officials and subjects who understood authority through that tradition. The proclamation announced the government he intended to build; it did not mean that his armies had already taken every claimed region.

sections.title: Eight more years of resistance
sections.text: Southern Song defended rivers and fortified positions. Overcoming those defences required supplies, sustained campaigning and expertise from several populations under Mongol command. Yuan and Song therefore existed at the same time. The change of dynasties was a prolonged military struggle, with the outcome still being fought over after the Yuan name had been announced.

cards.note: 1271–1279 covers the overlap between the Yuan proclamation and the final Southern Song conquest. It is part of Yuan history, not a separate dynasty.

sourceLabels.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongol_con: Wikipedia · Mongol conquest of the Song dynasty

dateReview.note: 1271–1279 is a defensible display interval between Yuan naming and Song conquest, not a distinct regime.

cards.significance: The Yuan proclamation shows that founding a dynasty was a political claim as well as a military achievement. Kublai adopted a Chinese dynastic name while Southern Song still resisted him, combining an imperial tradition familiar to Chinese officials with his Mongol authority. This helps explain why dynasties overlap on the timeline. A ruler could announce the order he intended to establish years before controlling all its claimed territory, and the work of conquest and government remained unfinished after the announcement.

significanceSources.label: The Metropolitan Museum of Art

image.alt: A painted portrait of Kublai Khan in a white robe and fur-trimmed hat.
image.caption: Kublai Khan’s portrait from the Yuan imperial album, traditionally associated with Araniko. It represents the ruler through court portraiture, rather than illustrating a specific proclamation.

cards.name: Early Qing
cards.description: Hong Taiji (皇太极) proclaimed the Qing dynasty in 1636, eight years before Qing forces entered Beijing (北京). His state had developed in the northeast, with connections reaching into Mongolia and Korea. The conquest of the Ming capital followed years of building armies, alliances and government.

sections.title: An established state before Beijing (北京)
sections.text: Manchu, Mongol and Han personnel served the emerging state through different military and administrative arrangements. Recruitment and defections brought soldiers and officials with useful skills. These people helped the rulers collect resources and govern. The force that entered Beijing (北京) in 1644 already belonged to a working state with institutions of its own.

sections.title: Two dates for the Qing
sections.text: The years 1636 and 1644 mark different steps. The first is the dynasty’s foundation; the second is its conquest of Beijing (北京) and adoption of the former Ming capital. Moving south greatly enlarged the dynasty’s ambitions and responsibilities. Its earlier relationships and institutions continued to shape Qing government. This short band shows the years when the Qing and the Ming court in Beijing (北京) coexisted.

cards.note: 1636–1644 is a concurrent exhibition segment, not a different Qing dynasty. The full Qing card preserves 1636; 1644 is stated prominently as the Beijing (北京) conquest.

sourceLabels.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of: Wikipedia · History of the Qing dynasty

dateReview.note: 1636 proclamation to 1644 Beijing conquest is a valid display interval, not a separate dynasty.

cards.significance: The Qing did not begin as an army suddenly arriving at the Ming capital. It already had a court, military organization and relationships with neighbouring peoples. Those earlier foundations helped it conquer and then govern a much larger realm. This changes how the transition looks: the Qing inherited Chinese imperial institutions, but also brought political traditions of its own. Its early northeastern history helps explain why the later dynasty governed through several languages, identities and kinds of authority.

significanceSources.label: UNESCO · Imperial palaces in Beijing and Shenyang

image.credit: J.H. Stewart Lockhart（骆克） · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: A printed illustration of both sides of a coin with Manchu writing.
image.caption: An 1895 numismatic illustration of a coin associated with Hong Taiji. The object’s Manchu inscription recalls Qing state formation before the conquest of Beijing; the illustration itself is much later.

cards.name: Southern Ming
cards.description: The fall of Beijing (北京) in 1644 did not end all Ming resistance. Princes and loyalist commanders established courts in the south and continued to challenge the Qing. Rival claims to the throne made cooperation difficult. The Yongli (永历) emperor’s death in 1662 marks the conventional end of the principal Southern Ming courts.

sections.title: Keeping a court alive
sections.text: A prince’s family connection to the Ming could support his claim to rule. He still needed soldiers, food, money and the loyalty of commanders. Southern Ming courts relied on regional forces whose leaders had interests of their own. Disagreements weakened resistance while Qing armies increased the military pressure. Holding a title offered little protection without the resources to defend it.

sections.title: Resistance beyond the courts
sections.text: The struggle extended beyond the main Southern Ming governments. The Zheng family’s maritime forces continued to invoke Ming authority and established a base in Taiwan (台湾). Their rule there lasted until 1683. The 1662 endpoint belongs to the principal claimant courts; resistance and attachment to the Ming continued after those courts had fallen.

cards.note: 1644–1662 covers the principal Southern Ming courts. Zheng rule in Taiwan (台湾) continued until 1683 and is not collapsed into this endpoint.

sourceLabels.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transition: Wikipedia · Transition from Ming to Qing

dateReview.note: 1644–1662 follows Lynn Struve's Cambridge chronology for the Southern Ming courts; the Taiwan continuation is properly distinguished.

cards.significance: The Southern Ming shows why a dynasty’s end rarely fits neatly into a single year. Losing the capital did not immediately erase loyalty, rival claims or the armies willing to defend them. The Qing had to win a prolonged contest for territory and cooperation. These surviving courts also connect the mainland conquest to maritime resistance and the Zheng family’s later base in Taiwan (台湾). The transition was a struggle among competing choices, with serious consequences for the people caught between them.

significanceSources.label: Cambridge History of China · The Southern Ming

image.alt: A fortified gateway with a large tower above the Great Wall.
image.caption: Shanhai Pass, photographed in 2009. The surviving and restored gateway marks a strategic setting associated with the Qing advance in 1644. This is the strategic gateway associated with the Qing advance, not a picture of Li Zicheng or a Southern Ming court.

cards.name: Republic of China in Taiwan (台湾)
cards.description: The Republic of China government relocated to Taiwan (台湾) in 1949 after defeat on the mainland. Taiwan (台湾) had come under ROC administration in 1945, following Japanese rule. The postwar years brought martial law and repression, alongside land reform and industrial growth. Later political movements helped transform the island’s government.
cards.note: 1949 marks relocation of the ROC government, not the start of Taiwan (台湾)’s history or an adjudication of contested sovereignty claims.

sections.title: Different histories meet
sections.text: Officials and refugees arriving from the mainland joined a population with its own experience of Qing and Japanese rule. They did not all share the same expectations or political position. The government’s claim to represent China shaped its policies, while local people experienced the effects of repression and rapid economic change. Taiwan (台湾)’s history cannot begin with the government’s arrival in 1949.

sections.title: Political change over decades
sections.text: Martial law was lifted in 1987, and Taiwan (台湾) held its first direct presidential election in 1996. Opposition groups, social movements and changes to institutions helped widen political participation. Economic growth accompanied this process, but did not make it inevitable. The Republic of China government continued through these changes; cross-strait political disputes also continued.

sourceLabels.https://1997-2001.state.gov/background_n: U.S. State Department · Taiwan historical background (2000)

dateReview.note: 1949 dates the relocation of the ROC central government to Taiwan. ROC administration of Taiwan began in 1945. 2026 is the exhibition horizon, not a historical end.

cards.significance: The relocation of the Republic’s government made the civil war’s outcome a lasting division across the Taiwan (台湾) Strait. The government continued in Taiwan (台湾), so 1949 cannot serve as the end of the Republic’s entire history. Taiwan (台湾)’s later political transformation also shows that the institutions brought there were not fixed forever. Its separate experience of authoritarian rule and democratization is necessary for understanding the different political systems on either side of the strait and the unresolved disagreements between them.

significanceSources.label: U.S. State Department · Taiwan historical background
Office of the President, ROC · Taiwan’s democratic transition

image.credit: Artist or photographer unidentified · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: Soldiers boarding a crowded vessel.
image.caption: Republic of China troops boarding a ship bound for Taiwan in 1949. A photograph of withdrawal captures one part of the relocation of the Nationalist state.

cards.name: Oracle-bone writing
cards.description: Late Shang diviners heated prepared animal bones or the lower shells of turtles, then interpreted the cracks as signs. Inscriptions could record a question, prediction and sometimes what happened. Especially at Anyang (安阳), these objects preserve the earliest large body of securely documented Chinese writing.
cards.catalogNote: 1200 BCE is an approximate representative date for surviving late-Shang inscriptions, not a dated invention of writing. The claim is earliest surviving substantial Chinese writing, not earliest writing worldwide.

sections.title: What worried a king
sections.text: Harvests, childbirth, weather and warfare appear alongside offerings to ancestors. Royal decisions involved both practical action and beliefs about ancestral powers. Repeated forms in the writing show that trained people prepared and kept these records. They give us unusually close contact with questions asked at the court.

sections.title: Writing already had a past
sections.text: A dated inscription shows that writing existed by then; it cannot tell us when writing began. Other materials survive less well, and the complicated script suggests earlier development that is hard to trace. These records also preserve a royal viewpoint. They cannot tell us everything ordinary people said or cared about, and many characters remain difficult to read.

cards.note: Ca. 1250 BCE is a reference point for the surviving late Shang corpus, not a proven invention year. Many characters and readings remain disputed.

dateReview.note: Existing c. 1250 BCE reference is appropriate for the earliest late-Shang corpus; do not force it back to the older workbook's c. 1200. No single invention year is established.

cards.significance: Oracle bones let modern readers test later accounts of Shang against the concerns and names recorded at its own court. They also connect the study of Chinese writing to a much longer history than the surviving paper book. Their significance is therefore double: they preserve an early stage of a continuing script tradition, and they change the evidence historians can use. Reading them reveals royal priorities directly, while reminding us that the survival of writing does not give every social group an equal voice.

significanceSources.label: University of Oxford · Inscribed oracle bones
Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art · Anyang

image.alt: A tortoise shell covered with columns of incised characters.
image.caption: An inscribed tortoise plastron from Anyang, around 1200 BCE, in the National Museum of China. The paired questions and numbered cracks make royal divination visible as a recorded procedure.

cards.name: Confucius (孔子)
cards.description: Confucius (孔子), traditionally dated 551–479 BCE, taught while Zhou kings lost power and noble families fought for influence. Teachings associated with him connect good government with learning, character and proper conduct. The Analects gathered these teachings across generations; it is not a word-for-word record made by the teacher himself.
cards.note: 551 BCE is the traditional birth date. The Analects contains different layers of writing, and the exact attribution of individual sayings remains debated.
cards.catalogNote: 551 BCE is the traditional birth date, not the date his philosophy arose. His traditional lifetime is 551–479 BCE. If figures use lifetime spans, adopt that range consistently.

sections.title: Learning how to behave
sections.text: Ritual meant more than performing a ceremony correctly. Conduct needed judgment and care for others, and repeated practice could help people develop those habits. Education therefore mattered to government. A ruler should first learn to control his own behaviour. Those serving him also had a duty to offer advice and, at times, criticism.

sections.title: Many later interpretations
sections.text: Later followers drew different lessons from these teachings, including personal improvement, family duties and the responsibility to challenge rulers. Imperial support gave some interpretations greater authority. The long history of Confucianism contains disagreements as well as shared texts. Later social hierarchies cannot all be treated as the direct wishes of one man.

dateReview.note: 551 BCE traditional birth is already correctly identified by title and note. No change needed.

cards.significance: Confucius (孔子) gave later generations a way to connect public government with the everyday cultivation of character. Learning, family responsibilities and the example of people in authority could all be discussed within one moral vocabulary. Schools and later imperial institutions helped carry that vocabulary far beyond his own circle. Its influence did not make Chinese society uniform: officials could use the same respected teachings to support a ruler or challenge his conduct. Knowing Confucius (孔子) helps explain why education became so closely connected with public authority.

significanceSources.label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy · Confucius

image.credit: Anonymous Chinese painter of the Western Han period · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: A faded painted human figure on an ancient plaster wall.
image.caption: A Western Han tomb fresco identified as Confucius, from Dongping in Shandong. Painted centuries after his lifetime, it testifies to his later authority rather than an authenticated likeness.

cards.name: Qin unification
cards.description: Qin’s conquest of Qi in 221 BCE completed its defeat of six major rival kingdoms. Ying Zheng (嬴政) took the title First Emperor. The conquered communities already had their own officials, customs and institutions. Qin now had to bring them under one ruler.
cards.catalogNote: 221 BCE marks completion of the conquests and formation of imperial Qin.

sections.title: After the armies won
sections.text: Qin extended its standards and appointed officials across the conquered territories. Local staff still had to register households, move supplies and interpret instructions. Defeating rival armies and governing their people were different tasks. The empire depended on directing existing networks of offices and workers toward the new emperor.

sections.title: Keeping the empire together
sections.text: The title First Emperor announced an authority intended to last. After his death in 210 BCE, struggles over succession exposed how fragile the government could be. Han later rebuilt a united empire using methods inherited from Qin. The conquest of 221 BCE established a model that later rulers would return to, even though Qin’s own ruling family could not preserve it.

cards.note: 221 BCE marks completion of the major conquests. “China unified” is shorthand for those kingdoms, not a claim that Qin controlled the borders of the present-day state.

sourceLabels.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qin%27s_wa: Wikipedia · Qin%27s wars of unification (reference overview)
sourceLabels.https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/441/: UNESCO · Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor

dateReview.note: 221 BCE marks completion of the conquests and formation of imperial Qin.

cards.significance: The conquest made a single emperor’s government the framework through which formerly independent kingdoms were to be ruled. That was a major change in political scale, but its longer importance depended on what followed: common administration could survive even when Qin’s own family lost power. Later rulers repeatedly treated broad imperial unity as a goal worth pursuing. The event marks the beginning of the imperial period on this atlas, while the continuing regional differences remind us that political unification never meant instant cultural uniformity.

significanceSources.label: UNESCO · Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor

image.alt: Rows of terracotta soldiers and a horse in a museum display.
image.caption: Terracotta figures from the First Emperor’s mausoleum complex. Their differentiated faces and equipment belong to a coordinated funerary project, not a surviving photograph of the Qin army.

cards.name: Papermaking advances
cards.description: Cai Lun (蔡伦), a court official, is traditionally credited with presenting an improved papermaking process in 105 CE. The account names bark, hemp waste, rags and fishing nets among the materials. Older paper has been excavated, so his achievement was an improvement recognized at court, rather than the first invention of paper.
cards.note: 105 CE is the traditional report date. Earlier finds disprove a literal first-invention claim; the date when paper became dominant varied by place and use.

sections.title: A more convenient writing material
sections.text: Paper could be lighter than bamboo or wooden writing strips and cheaper than silk. It offered new possibilities for copying texts and sending letters, and later for printing. Older materials did not disappear immediately. Writers needed a reliable supply of usable paper, which depended on skilled workers as well as a recipe.

sections.title: The workers behind the name
sections.text: Cai Lun (蔡伦)’s court connection helped preserve his name in written history. The many craftspeople who developed paper are harder to identify. Paper spread through repeated improvements and exchanges between people. Its movement westward cannot be fully explained by one inventor or one famous battle. Different places adopted it for different uses over time.

dateReview.note: 105 CE traditional improvement/report date is correct as qualified. Smithsonian bibliographic abstract confirms paper existed before 105. Existing Iranica page concerns Persian papermaking and does not directly evidence 105; replace or supplement with direct Cai Lun evidence.

cards.significance: As paper became more widely available, written material became easier to make, transport and keep than bundles of wooden or bamboo slips, and less costly than silk. That helped support the long expansion of administration, religious copying and literary exchange. Later printing multiplied those possibilities, but required its own developments centuries afterward. Cai Lun (蔡伦)’s place in this story is a recognized improvement within a collective technological history. The larger consequence came through repeated production and adoption, not a single inventor transforming literacy overnight.

significanceSources.label: Encyclopaedia Iranica · Paper and papermaking

image.alt: A fragile light-brown fragment of early paper.
image.caption: A Western Han hemp-paper fragment. Its survival helps distinguish papermaking before Cai Lun from the improvement and court presentation traditionally associated with him in 105.

cards.name: Sui reunification
cards.description: Sui forces conquered the southern Chen dynasty in 589. The victory brought the lower Yangtze (长江) and other southern regions under the northern court, ending a major political division.
cards.catalogNote: 589 marks Sui conquest of Chen and reunification; distinct from Sui foundation in 581.

sections.title: Governing the conquered regions
sections.text: Defeating a rival emperor did not make local officials and communities disappear. Sui needed appointments, cooperation and dependable ways to gather and move supplies. These were slower tasks than capturing a capital. Political reunification began a larger effort to make northern and southern government work together.

sections.title: What the south brought
sections.text: Southern courts had spent centuries developing their own institutions and cultural life. Sui inherited regions with established resources, skills and powerful local relationships. The reunited empire depended on these foundations while redirecting them toward a new imperial centre. Southern history did not begin with the northern conquest.

sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs: Arthur Wright · The Sui Dynasty
Cambridge History of China · Southern dynasties

cards.note: 589 dates Chen’s conquest, not Sui’s foundation in 581 or immediate completion of all regional integration.

dateReview.note: 589 marks Sui conquest of Chen and reunification; distinct from Sui foundation in 581.

cards.significance: The conquest of Chen created the territorial foundation on which Sui and Tang could join northern political power to southern resources. Its consequences depended on what followed: moving supplies, incorporating officials and governing communities with their own traditions. Reunification therefore meant more than restoring a familiar outline on a map. It brought regions transformed by centuries of separate development into a new relationship. That relationship became increasingly important as the south's economic weight grew within later empires.

significanceSources.label: Arthur Wright · The Sui Dynasty
Cambridge History of China · Southern dynasties

image.alt: Two long swords with decorated hilts.
image.caption: Two swords dated around 600, in the Metropolitan Museum of Art, reportedly found near Luoyang. Their date places them in the Sui period; their specific archaeological provenance is reported rather than secure.

cards.name: An Lushan Rebellion (安史之乱)
cards.description: An Lushan (安禄山)’s revolt began in December 755 and grew into a prolonged civil war. Tang forces defeated the main rebellion by 763, but the government that survived had a different balance of power between the emperor and provincial commanders.
cards.note: 755 marks the outbreak; the main rebellion continued until 763. Losses in tax registers include people the government could no longer count and cannot be read directly as a death toll.
cards.catalogNote: 755 is the onset; the rebellion continued to 763. Keep point at onset; describe 755–763 in summary.

sections.title: Saving the dynasty strengthened commanders
sections.text: The court created more military commands to organize resistance. Many provincial armies fought for Tang, so stronger regional military power grew partly from the effort to save it. Commanders needed soldiers, supplies and dependable income. Once they controlled these resources, the emperor could not simply take every wartime power back.

sections.title: Government after the war
sections.text: The restored court increasingly raised money through taxes on commerce and consumption. These changes helped support continued government, even as powerful provinces limited what the emperor could demand. Tang lasted for another century and a half, with important cultural achievements as well as conflict. Survival required compromises that both sustained the dynasty and constrained it.

dateReview.note: 755 is the onset; the rebellion continued to 763. Keep point at onset; describe 755–763 in summary.

cards.significance: The rebellion changed how Tang could govern. To defeat it, the court relied on commanders whose troops and resources could not simply be brought back under earlier controls. New ways of raising revenue helped compensate for lost authority, keeping the dynasty alive while changing its relationship with provinces and taxpayers. This connects the war to the different political and economic arrangements of later Tang. Its significance is a transformation of imperial power through survival, not a single disaster that made every later outcome inevitable.

significanceSources.label: David Graff · The Reach of the Military: Tang
Cambridge Economic History · Public Finance

image.alt: A long calligraphic manuscript with corrections and crossings-out.
image.caption: Yan Zhenqing’s Draft of a Requiem to My Nephew, dated 758. Its corrections preserve an act of mourning within the An Lushan Rebellion (安史之乱), linking political violence to a family’s loss.

cards.name: Diamond Sutra
cards.description: The Diamond Sutra scroll dated 868 is an exceptionally early surviving printed book. Its dedication names Wang Jie (王玠) as the sponsor. He had the Buddhist scripture made for his parents’ benefit and for wider distribution.
cards.note: An exceptionally early dated printed book. Printing itself predates this scroll.

sections.title: Printing for religious merit
sections.text: Making copies of a scripture could spread Buddhist teaching and bring religious merit to the donor and others. Wang Jie (王玠)’s dedication connects the printed object to his family and to readers beyond it. The reason to reproduce a text mattered as much as the method: religious giving helped create demand for copies.

sections.title: A date we can trust
sections.text: The dedication gives this surviving scroll a clear place in time. Printing already existed before 868, so the date does not mark its invention. What survives is a particular act of sponsorship, bringing together a sacred text, skilled production and a named donor. It offers a close view of how printing served religious life.

sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/: David Graff · The Reach of the Military: Tang

cards.significance: This scroll reveals a practical connection between belief and the spread of knowledge. Donors wanted religious texts reproduced for others, giving printers a reason to make many copies of the same words and images. That demand belongs to the longer history in which printing expanded access to books and learning. The dated dedication lets us see one household's contribution to that process. A surviving object cannot identify printing's first moment, but it can show why people invested in its use.

significanceSources.label: British Library · Diamond Sutra

image.credit: Anonymous Tang printers; commissioned by Wang Jie · British Library
image.alt: A printed Buddhist assembly above columns of Chinese text.
image.caption: The frontispiece of the Diamond Sutra dated 868, now in the British Library. Its survival makes the relationship between devotion, sponsorship, and woodblock reproduction unusually concrete. The 868 object uses woodblock printing; it must not be mistaken for a surviving example of Bi Sheng’s later movable type.

cards.name: Treaty of Chanyuan (澶渊)
cards.description: In 1005, Song and Liao agreed to end a period of frontier warfare. Song promised annual payments of silver and silk, and the two courts recognized one another’s imperial standing. The settlement made coexistence possible without either side conquering the other.
cards.catalogNote: Mid-January 1005 oath exchange follows the winter campaign of 1004; use 1005 in converted Common Era chronology.

sections.title: The cost of peace
sections.text: Annual payments were easy to criticize, but war also required money for armies and garrisons and disrupted livelihoods along the border. The treaty offered a way to secure the frontier through negotiation. Accepting another emperor meant placing practical limits on each court’s claims to supreme authority.

sections.title: A durable but changeable agreement
sections.text: Repeated embassies and more predictable relations followed. Rivalry and border disputes did not vanish, and the agreement depended on a changing regional balance of power. Song later allied with Jin against Liao, helping overturn the order that the treaty had supported. A century of relative peace was a significant achievement, but it did not make the settlement permanent.

cards.note: 1005 uses the converted common-era year; the agreement followed the winter campaign of 1004. Peace was relative, not the absence of every frontier dispute.

sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/: Paul Jakov Smith · The fragility of the Chanyuan peace

dateReview.note: Mid-January 1005 oath exchange follows the winter campaign of 1004; use 1005 in converted Common Era chronology.

cards.significance: Chanyuan (澶渊) shows why durable peace belongs in Chinese history alongside conquest and reunification. By making coexistence workable, it helped sustain a world with several imperial courts rather than bringing every territory under one ruler. The long interval without major Song–Liao war gave this diplomatic achievement consequences for generations of border inhabitants. Annual transfers and repeated embassies made security a relationship to maintain, not simply a victory to win. The settlement did not end Song's military spending or permanently erase ambitions in the north, and prosperity had causes beyond the treaty. Song's later alliance with Jin against Liao helped undo this order, showing how a bid to recover territory could destroy an arrangement that had provided security.

significanceSources.label: Paul Jakov Smith · The fragility of the Chanyuan peace

image.alt: An elaborate gold-coloured crown with pierced ornament.
image.caption: A gilt-silver Khitan crown from the tomb of the Princess of Chen State and her husband, early eleventh century. The object makes Liao elite ceremonial culture visible.

cards.name: Fall of Kaifeng (开封)
cards.description: Jin forces captured Kaifeng (开封) in 1127. They took Emperor Qinzong (宋钦宗), the retired Emperor Huizong (宋徽宗) and members of the Song court north as prisoners. Northern Song ended, but a surviving prince established a new Song court that same year.
cards.catalogNote: 1127 dates Northern Song's fall and imperial captivity, at the culmination of the 1126–1127 crisis.

sections.title: An alliance backfires
sections.text: Song had joined the rising Jin against Liao, hoping to recover territory. Once Liao was defeated, Song faced a more dangerous neighbour. Removing an old rival had also removed a state that stood between Song and another expanding power. The earlier alliance left Song in a much more difficult position.

sections.title: Rebuilding in the south
sections.text: Officials and refugees carried skills, possessions and memories south. A new court drew on the region’s existing economic strength to rebuild government. The captive emperors complicated the new ruler’s claim to authority, and recovering the north remained a charged political issue. Southern Song preserved the dynasty while changing its territory, resources and relationship with its northern enemy.

cards.note: 1127 marks Kaifeng (开封)’s fall and the emperors’ captivity after campaigns in 1125–1127. Song continued in the south until 1279.

dateReview.note: 1127 dates Northern Song's fall and imperial captivity, at the culmination of the 1126–1127 crisis.

cards.significance: The capture of Kaifeng (开封) changed the geography of Song government and made recovery of the north a lasting political cause. Yet the dynasty’s survival depended in part on southern regions that already possessed the people, production and transport needed to support another court. The catastrophe therefore connects diplomatic miscalculation with the south's growing importance in Chinese history. It also exposes a recurring danger in alliances: defeating Liao alongside Jin removed an old adversary without creating a secure relationship with the stronger power that replaced it.

significanceSources.label: Metropolitan Museum · China, 1000–1400
Paul Jakov Smith · The Fragility of Peace

image.credit: Emperor Huizong of Song (1082–1135) · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: Cranes circling above a palace roof in a painted sky.
image.caption: Auspicious Cranes, associated with Emperor Huizong of Song. The courtly vision of an auspicious capital is particularly revealing when read alongside the political disaster of 1127.

cards.name: Ming Voyages
cards.description: Zheng He (郑和)’s first fleet departed in 1405. It began seven Ming-sponsored expeditions that continued until 1433, linking the imperial court with ports across Southeast Asia and the Indian Ocean. The fleets eventually reached the East African coast, travelling along routes already used by merchants and sailors.

sections.title: Gifts, trade and military power
sections.text: The ships carried envoys, gifts and commercial goods, as well as troops. The expeditions displayed the emperor’s wealth and power and sometimes intervened in local conflicts. Their journeys depended on existing knowledge of navigation and the port communities they visited. These were ambitious state voyages through a connected maritime world.

sections.title: What happened when the fleets stopped?
sections.text: The Ming court eventually stopped funding these enormous official expeditions as its spending priorities changed. Chinese merchants continued to travel and trade by sea. The end of the fleets was therefore one change within a much larger history of maritime activity. The date on this card, 1405, marks the first departure; it does not date the whole series of voyages.

cards.note: 1405 marks the first departure; the seven-expedition programme extended to 1433. The largest ship-size claims remain contested and are not used here.

sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/: Journal of Chinese History · Official voyages and private sailings

dateReview.note: 1405 is the first departure. The existing note appropriately explains the seven-voyage sequence through 1433.

cards.significance: The voyages make an important distinction visible: possessing the ability to project power overseas was different from choosing to sustain it. The Ming court also faced costly demands on its northern frontier and at its new capital. Ships, skilled crews and trading connections did not by themselves determine imperial priorities. This helps explain a larger pattern in Chinese history: a society could be closely connected to overseas commerce while its rulers concentrated resources on defending and governing a continental empire.

significanceSources.label: Columbia University · The Ming voyages
Journal of Chinese History · The cessation of Zheng He’s voyages

image.alt: A tall stone slab with three blocks of inscriptions.
image.caption: The Galle trilingual inscription associated with Zheng He, dated 1409. Chinese, Tamil, and Persian texts place maritime diplomacy within several religious and linguistic worlds.

cards.name: Treaty of Nanking (南京)
cards.description: The Treaty of Nanking (南京) ended the First Opium War in 1842. The Qing ceded Hong Kong (香港) Island to Britain, agreed to pay a large sum of money and opened five ports to British trade and residence. The settlement gave lasting force to demands made through military pressure.

sections.title: From one treaty to a wider system
sections.text: Later agreements added foreign privileges, including arrangements that placed foreigners outside parts of Qing legal authority. Other powers sought similar treatment. These terms accumulated over time. They affected where foreigners could live and trade, which courts could judge disputes and how officials dealt with foreign residents. The later provisions should be distinguished from the original 1842 treaty.

sections.title: Trade on imposed terms
sections.text: Chinese merchants had traded overseas long before the war. The treaty changed the terms on which foreign powers could demand access to Chinese ports. Britain used military victory to secure commercial and territorial concessions. Qing government continued, but its control over foreign activity was reduced. The treaty itself did not legalize the opium trade.

cards.note: 1842: Treaty of Nanking (南京). Extraterritoriality was elaborated in subsequent agreements; the treaty did not itself legalize the opium trade.

sourceLabels.https://history.state.gov/milestones/183: U.S. Office of the Historian · Opium War and treaty system

dateReview.note: 1842 is confirmed for the treaty; the distinction between this treaty and subsequent privileges is appropriate.

cards.significance: The treaty turned a British military victory into enduring limits on Qing control over trade and territory. Opening treaty ports and ceding Hong Kong (香港) created arrangements that later agreements expanded, including additional foreign privileges. For people living in these ports, international power now shaped local commerce and administration more directly. This is why the agreement matters beyond the end of one war: it helped establish the treaty system that later reformers and revolutionaries sought to dismantle. Not every later privilege originated in this treaty itself.

significanceSources.label: U.S. Office of the Historian · The opening to China

image.alt: A silver coin stamped with several small Chinese marks.
image.caption: A Mexican Spanish dollar dated 1796, bearing Chinese merchant chop marks. This later coin illustrates the long-lived silver trade, not a coin documented on the first Manila galleon. The nineteenth-century treaty imposed an indemnity denominated in silver dollars; this 1796 coin is a comparable circulating monetary object, not a coin from the payment.

cards.name: End of Imperial China
cards.description: On 12 February 1912, the child emperor Puyi (溥仪) abdicated and Qing rule ended. The Republic of China had already been founded on 1 January. Negotiations among revolutionaries, the court and military leaders brought the monarchy to an end, following the uprising of 1911.

sections.title: A settlement backed by military power
sections.text: Yuan Shikai (袁世凯) commanded forces essential to the court’s survival. Sun Yat-sen (孙中山) agreed to give up the provisional presidency in his favour as part of the settlement. The new republic therefore depended partly on men who had gained power under the Qing. Its civilian leaders still faced the problem of controlling armies and the commanders who led them.

sections.title: A new government, a longer transition
sections.text: Abdication ended the dynasty, but changing the institutions and habits of government took longer. The republic promised citizenship and representative government while officials and military leaders competed for authority. Under the settlement, Puyi (溥仪) continued to live in the Forbidden City until 1924. His departure from power and his departure from the palace were separate events.

sourceLabels.https://history.state.gov/countries/chin: U.S. Office of the Historian · Recognition and diplomatic relations
sourceLabels.https://history.state.gov/historicaldocu: U.S. diplomatic documents · Abdication and republican transition, 1912

cards.note: Qing abdication: 12 February 1912. The Republic was founded earlier, on 1 January 1912. Puyi (溥仪) remained in the Forbidden City until 1924.

dateReview.note: Qing abdication occurred on 12 February 1912, after the ROC provisional government was established on 1 January.

cards.significance: Abdication closed the long era in which a hereditary emperor stood at the centre of government. It also required negotiation over how authority, territory and obligations would pass to a republic. Removing the throne did not settle who could govern effectively or how citizens would hold rulers accountable. Those questions drove much of the twentieth century’s political struggle. The importance of 1912 therefore lies in both a clear institutional ending and the difficult work of building a different political order.

significanceSources.label: U.S. Office of the Historian · The revolution and republican transition

image.alt: Sun Yat-sen and Li Yuanhong standing together in formal dress.
image.caption: Sun Yat-sen and Li Yuanhong at Wuchang in April 1912. Their encounter belongs to the early republic’s effort to convert revolutionary coalitions into a functioning state.
