cards.name: Beijing (北京) Becomes the Qing Capital
cards.description: Qing forces entered Beijing (北京) in 1644. Li Zicheng (李自成)’s rebels had already captured the city, and the Ming emperor had died. The Qing made the former Ming capital their own, eight years after proclaiming their dynasty in the northeast.
cards.note: 1644 marks Beijing (北京)’s conquest and adoption as Qing capital. It is distinct from the 1636 dynastic foundation and from the later completion of territorial consolidation.

sections.title: Taking over the imperial capital
sections.text: The palaces, offices and ceremonies of Beijing (北京) helped the new rulers claim the authority of emperors. They presented themselves as successors to the Ming while criticizing its failures. Familiar institutions helped officials and residents deal with the new court. The ruling family had changed, but much of the machinery and symbolism of imperial government remained useful.

sections.title: The war continued elsewhere
sections.text: Possession of Beijing (北京) gave the Qing an important centre of government. Ming princes and loyalist armies still resisted in the south, and the conquest continued. The Qing also retained military and political arrangements developed before taking the city. Its move to Beijing (北京) was a major turning point within a longer expansion, rather than the moment when every region accepted its rule.

sourceLabels.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transition: Wikipedia · Transition from Ming to Qing

dateReview.note: 1644 dates the Qing court's move to Beijing; Qing was proclaimed in 1636, and territorial conquest continued after 1644.

cards.catalogNote: 1644 dates the Qing court's move to Beijing; Qing was proclaimed in 1636, and territorial conquest continued after 1644.
cards.significance: By occupying the Ming capital and its palace, the Qing could present conquest as succession to an established imperial order. Buildings, ceremonies and government offices provided practical tools for that claim. Yet the new rulers also retained Manchu institutions and connections with their northeastern homeland. Beijing (北京) therefore helps explain both continuity and change across 1644: much of the machinery of rule survived, while the people directing it and the wider realm they would govern changed substantially.

significanceSources.label: Columbia University · Qing government and claims to succession
UNESCO · Imperial palaces

image.alt: A painted portrait of Dorgon in formal court robes.
image.caption: A seventeenth-century portrait of Dorgon. The regent’s image accompanies the Qing conquest of Beijing in 1644, which was distinct from the dynasty’s foundation in 1636.

cards.name: Ming Palace Eunuchs
cards.description: Eunuchs served inside the Ming palace, but some also became military commanders, administrators and imperial envoys. Their responsibilities expanded under the Yongle (永乐) Emperor and later rulers. Access to the emperor could give a palace attendant influence far beyond the imperial household.
cards.note: Circa 1403–1424 is the Yongle (永乐) reign era, used here to show an expansion of eunuch roles. Yongle (永乐) took power in 1402. The change developed over time.

sections.title: A second route to the emperor
sections.text: An emperor could give trusted attendants tasks that would otherwise pass through regular officials. This offered another source of information and another way to issue orders. It also gave attendants opportunities to control access and promote supporters. Palace service became part of a wider struggle over who could advise the ruler and carry out his decisions.

sections.title: Different people, different roles
sections.text: Zheng He (郑和) led overseas expeditions; Wei Zhongxian (魏忠贤) later built a powerful court network that persecuted opponents. Their shared status as eunuchs does not explain their different careers. Scholar-officials often wrote hostile accounts of eunuch power, while also competing with them for influence. Each career is best understood through the responsibilities and powers the emperor granted.

sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/cam: Cambridge History of China · Ming institutional history

dateReview.note: The exact 1400 marker is unsupported. Proposed circa 1403 is an editorial anchor for expansion under Yongle: accession 1402, reign era 1403–1424. This was a continuing institutional process, not a single decree.

cards.catalogNote: The exact 1400 marker is unsupported. Proposed circa 1403 is an editorial anchor for expansion under Yongle: accession 1402, reign era 1403–1424. This was a continuing institutional process, not a single decree.
searchAliases: Expansion of eunuch power in Ming government
cards.significance: Eunuchs gave emperors a channel for carrying out orders alongside the regular civil service. Their roles in administration, military affairs and overseas missions show that imperial government depended on more than examination-trained officials. Cooperation could make the system function, while competition for access to the ruler could distort decisions. This helps explain recurring struggles at the Ming court without reducing them to a simple story of good scholars and bad eunuchs. Many eunuchs performed routine work; a few acquired extraordinary power.

significanceSources.label: Cambridge History of China · Ming government and eunuchs

image.credit: Artist or photographer unidentified · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: An emperor seated in a yellow robe and black headdress.
image.caption: A formal portrait of the Yongle emperor. It provides a courtly image of the ruler associated with the transfer of the Ming capital to Beijing and Zheng He’s voyages. The emperor’s portrait provides context for palace service and imperial delegation; it does not depict a eunuch.

cards.name: Wei Zhongxian (魏忠贤)’s Court Power
cards.description: Wei Zhongxian (魏忠贤) gained exceptional influence during the Tianqi (天启) emperor’s reign. He used access to the palace and allies among officials to build a powerful network. In 1624, the official Yang Lian (杨涟) publicly denounced him. Persecution of critics associated with the Donglin movement followed.
cards.note: 1624 is the inherited focal year of confrontation, not the beginning of all Wei’s influence. His fall and death came in 1627. Hostile accounts of his early life require caution.

sections.title: Power through access
sections.text: The ability to influence what the emperor heard could affect appointments and careers across government. Wei relied on officials outside the palace as well as other attendants. Some joined his network, while others resisted or tried to work around it. His power grew through these connections and the emperor’s protection, rather than through one formal title.

sections.title: A change of emperor
sections.text: Tianqi (天启) died in 1627. Under the new Chongzhen (崇祯) emperor, Wei lost his protection and his position collapsed. His fall showed how closely his influence had depended on favour at court. It also followed years of harm to opponents. The 1624 date marks a major confrontation during his rise; his fall and death came three years later.

dateReview.note: 1624 is a supported focal year: Yang Lian's memorial denouncing Wei is dated Tianqi 4. Wei's influence began earlier; major persecutions followed in 1625–1626 and his fall and death in 1627.

cards.catalogNote: 1624 is a supported focal year: Yang Lian's memorial denouncing Wei is dated Tianqi 4. Wei's influence began earlier; major persecutions followed in 1625–1626 and his fall and death in 1627.
cards.significance: Wei Zhongxian (魏忠贤)’s influence exposes a weakness in government organized around access to an emperor. Officials’ careers and their ability to criticize policy could depend on powerful intermediaries close to the throne. His rise and fall therefore matter beyond his personal reputation: they show how court relationships could disrupt the institutions intended to advise and restrain rulers. These conflicts contributed to the troubled politics of the late Ming, although explaining the dynasty’s collapse requires looking beyond one eunuch to war, rebellion and finance.

significanceSources.label: Palace Museum · The Tianqi emperor
Cambridge History of China · Ming government

image.alt: Several painted porcelain cups displayed together.
image.caption: Porcelain teacups from the Tianqi reign, 1621–1627. These are objects from the period of Wei Zhongxian’s influence, not evidence that he personally commissioned them.

cards.name: First Opium War
cards.description: In 1839, Qing commissioner Lin Zexu (林则徐) moved to suppress the illegal opium trade. Conflict with Britain followed. British naval and land forces, including troops from India, attacked coastal and river positions. The war ended in 1842 with the Treaty of Nanking (南京).
cards.note: 1839–1842 includes the initial clashes; 1840–1842 is also used for the main expedition. The 1842 treaty did not itself legalize opium or establish all later foreign privileges.

sections.title: Opium, tea and overseas trade
sections.text: Merchants used opium grown in British India to help finance purchases of Chinese tea. This trade connected Indian production, Chinese buyers and British demand. Qing efforts to stop the imports challenged a profitable business while confronting the damage caused by addiction. Britain intervened militarily and pressed for wider access to Chinese markets.

sections.title: The terms of defeat
sections.text: British forces advanced along the Yangtze (长江) toward Nanjing (南京). The resulting treaty opened five ports, required payments and ceded Hong Kong (香港) Island to Britain. Later agreements added further foreign privileges. These concessions limited the Qing government’s control over foreign activity. The treaty did not itself legalize opium. The dates 1839–1842 include the initial clashes; some accounts use 1840 for the main British expedition.

sourceLabels.https://www.nam.ac.uk/explore/first-chin: National Army Museum · First China War
sourceLabels.https://history.state.gov/milestones/183: U.S. Office of the Historian · Opium War and treaty system

dateReview.note: 1839 is a start-year marker for the 1839–1842 war. It includes initial clashes; some periodizations begin with the main expedition in 1840.

cards.catalogNote: 1839 is a start-year marker for the 1839–1842 war. It includes initial clashes; some periodizations begin with the main expedition in 1840.
cards.significance: The war exposed a dangerous gap between Qing authority over its own trade rules and its ability to defend those rules against British force. Defeat gave Britain the means to demand ports, money and territory. The resulting treaty arrangements made foreign pressure a continuing part of Qing government rather than an isolated military emergency. For later generations, the conflict became a reference point in arguments about sovereignty and national weakness, although the dynasty’s subsequent crises also had powerful domestic causes.

significanceSources.label: National Army Museum · First China War
U.S. Office of the Historian · China and the treaty system

cards.name: Taiping Rebellion
cards.description: Hong Xiuquan (洪秀全)’s religious movement became a vast civil war against the Qing. Hong claimed to be Jesus’s younger brother and established a Heavenly Kingdom. His forces captured Nanjing (南京) in 1853 and made it their capital. Qing armies retook the city in 1864 after years of devastating war.
cards.note: 1850–1864 covers the broader conflict; 1851 marks the formal proclamation at Jintian. Resistance continued after Nanjing (南京) fell. Death estimates include famine and disease as well as direct violence and remain highly uncertain.

sections.title: A rival government
sections.text: The Taiping challenged Manchu rule and proposed sweeping changes to property and social life. Religious beliefs gave the movement a shared cause, while hardship and local conflict helped it recruit followers. Its leaders promised equality, but their state also had powerful hierarchies and violent internal struggles. The rules they announced and the lives people experienced under wartime government could differ greatly.

sections.title: The cost of civil war
sections.text: The Qing increasingly relied on regional armies raised by officials such as Zeng Guofan (曾国藩). Local recruitment and finance helped sustain the forces that defeated the Taiping. This strengthened provincial military networks within Qing government. Fighting, famine and disease devastated southern and central regions. The death toll remains highly uncertain, and resistance continued after the fall of Nanjing (南京).

sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/: Journal of Institutional Economics · Regional armies and Qing survival

dateReview.note: 1850 is a defensible start for the broader 1850–1864 civil war; 1851 is used for formal uprising/proclamation. Nanjing fell in July 1864; surviving resistance lasted longer.

cards.catalogNote: 1850 is a defensible start for the broader 1850–1864 civil war; 1851 is used for formal uprising/proclamation. Nanjing fell in July 1864; surviving resistance lasted longer.
cards.significance: Suppressing the rebellion kept the Qing on the throne, but changed the resources on which its survival depended. Regional leaders raised armies and funds that the regular imperial forces could not supply effectively. These new arrangements helped restore order while giving provincial military networks greater importance. The war also devastated communities and productive land. It therefore connects two major strands of later Qing history: attempts to rebuild the country and the growing difficulty of keeping military and financial power under central direction.

significanceSources.label: Cambridge History of China · The Qing restoration

image.caption: Wu Youru’s depiction of the recovery of Ruizhou, dated 1886. Made after the Taiping war, it presents a Qing victory narrative rather than an eyewitness record of combat.

cards.name: Second Opium War
cards.description: Britain and France fought the Qing from 1856 to 1860 to obtain further commercial and diplomatic concessions. Their forces eventually occupied Beijing (北京). They looted the Old Summer Palace, and British troops burned it. The defeat forced the Qing to accept a wider foreign presence.
cards.note: 1856–1860 covers several campaigns and negotiations. The Old Summer Palace was Yuanmingyuan (圆明园), a separate site from the Forbidden City.

sections.title: Fighting over access
sections.text: Britain used the Arrow incident in Canton as its immediate reason for intervention; France invoked the execution of a missionary. The Treaties of Tianjin (天津) in 1858 provided for more treaty ports and foreign diplomats in Beijing (北京). Disputes over carrying out those terms led to renewed fighting and the Conventions of Beijing (北京) in 1860.

sections.title: A government under pressure
sections.text: The settlement expanded foreign privileges and required further payments. Associated trade arrangements legalized opium imports. At the same time, the Qing was fighting the Taiping civil war. Military defeat abroad and rebellion at home placed heavy demands on its money and armies. The destroyed Old Summer Palace was Yuanmingyuan (圆明园), a separate site from the Forbidden City.

sourceLabels.https://www.nam.ac.uk/explore/second-chi: National Army Museum · Second China War
sourceLabels.https://history.state.gov/milestones/183: U.S. Office of the Historian · Opium War and treaty system

dateReview.note: 1856 is the starting marker for the 1856–1860 conflict, which comprised several campaigns and negotiations.

cards.catalogNote: 1856 is the starting marker for the 1856–1860 conflict, which comprised several campaigns and negotiations.
cards.significance: This war deepened the treaty system and demonstrated that foreign armies could reach the imperial capital itself. Expanded privileges and a permanent diplomatic presence made dealings with foreign powers harder for the court to contain at a distance. The destruction of the Old Summer Palace gave the defeat an enduring place in historical memory. Together with the civil wars of the same era, these pressures made military reform and new ways of conducting foreign relations urgent questions for Qing officials.

significanceSources.label: National Army Museum · Second China War
Columbia University · Reform in the nineteenth century

image.caption: A Canton River scene associated with the fighting of 1857. Thomas Goldsworthy Dutton painted it after sketches by naval officer Albert Denison; the series was probably commissioned in the early 1860s. It is a later artistic treatment of a wartime setting.

cards.name: Self-Strengthening Movement
cards.description: Qing officials responded to military defeats and civil war with projects to strengthen the state. From the 1860s, they built arsenals and shipyards, opened language schools and supported new industries. These efforts are usually grouped under the name Self-Strengthening Movement.
cards.note: Circa 1861–1895 is a conventional frame for the Self-Strengthening Movement. Its proposals and institutions developed at different dates; some histories use the broader 1860s–1890s.

sections.title: More than buying new weapons
sections.text: Modern ships and guns needed trained crews, maintenance, reliable supplies and money. Translation and education became important parts of military rebuilding. Officials such as Li Hongzhang (李鸿章) also supported transport and commercial ventures. The aim was to develop the skills and resources needed to defend the country, as well as obtain foreign equipment.

sections.title: Projects with different results
sections.text: Different officials sponsored different enterprises. Some developed useful skills and infrastructure, while others struggled with funding and coordination. The movement did not operate as one centrally managed programme. Defeat by Japan in 1894–1895 intensified criticism and demands for deeper political change. The conventional dates, around 1861–1895, cover many projects that began and developed at different times.

sourceLabels.https://afe.easia.columbia.edu/special/c: Columbia University · From reform to revolution

dateReview.note: Propose circa 1861 as the start anchor, rather than an exact 1860 event. The movement developed from earlier proposals and continued into the 1894–1895 war; scholarly period boundaries vary.

cards.catalogNote: Propose circa 1861 as the start anchor, rather than an exact 1860 event. The movement developed from earlier proposals and continued into the 1894–1895 war; scholarly period boundaries vary.
cards.significance: Self-strengthening was an attempt to preserve imperial government by changing the tools it used. Arsenals, shipyards, language training and other projects brought new expertise into institutions built around older priorities. Their uneven results made reformers ask whether buying weapons was enough, or whether education and government also had to change. These experiments helped develop skills and organizations used later, even though they did not prevent further defeats. Their significance lies in opening practical paths to change while revealing the limits of the existing state.

significanceSources.label: Columbia University · China’s nineteenth-century reform efforts

image.credit: Artist or photographer unidentified · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: A group portrait of Qing officials in formal dress.
image.caption: Members of the Zongli Yamen in 1894, in a photographic engraving. The institution embodied the Qing effort to manage foreign affairs through new diplomatic machinery.

cards.name: First Sino-Japanese War
cards.description: The First Sino-Japanese War began in 1894 over influence in Korea. Qing forces suffered defeats on land and at sea. The 1895 Treaty of Shimonoseki required a large payment and transferred Taiwan (台湾) and the Penghu (澎湖) Islands to Japan. The outcome shook confidence in Qing military reforms.
cards.note: 1894–1895 covers the war. Resistance to Japanese conquest in Taiwan (台湾) continued after the April 1895 treaty.

sections.title: War over Korea
sections.text: Intervention in a Korean political crisis brought China and Japan into conflict. Korea had its own political struggles, and its people faced the consequences of both powers’ ambitions. Fighting spread from Korea into Manchuria and coastal naval bases. Japan’s victory ended Qing claims in Korea while strengthening Japan’s own expansion in the region.

sections.title: The consequences of defeat
sections.text: The Qing borrowed money to meet the treaty’s financial demands, adding to its burdens. Reformers questioned whether new ships and weapons were enough without wider changes in government. In Taiwan (台湾), Japanese conquest met resistance after the treaty was signed. The diplomatic transfer and the establishment of Japanese control were different stages, with different consequences for the people living there.

sourceLabels.https://visualizingcultures.mit.edu/thro: John W. Dower, MIT · Sino-Japanese War and visual propaganda
John W. Dower, MIT · Spoils of war

dateReview.note: 1894 is the start-year marker for the First Sino-Japanese War of 1894–1895.

cards.catalogNote: 1894 is the start-year marker for the First Sino-Japanese War of 1894–1895.
cards.significance: Defeat by Japan challenged the hope that selective military modernization had made the Qing secure. The settlement changed the balance of power in East Asia, including the loss of Taiwan (台湾) and the end of Qing claims to Korea’s dependence. It also gave reformers a powerful argument that deeper institutional change was necessary. The war links domestic reform debates with the rise of Japanese imperial expansion, which would place much greater pressure on China in the following decades.

significanceSources.label: MIT Visualizing Cultures · The Sino-Japanese War

image.alt: An armoured steam warship with two masts.
image.caption: Dingyuan, flagship of the Beiyang Fleet. Its modern equipment makes the defeat of 1894–1895 a question of institutions, command, and strategy as well as technology.

cards.name: Hundred Days Reform
cards.description: In 1898, the Guangxu (光绪) emperor supported a rapid series of reforms associated with Kang Youwei (康有为), Liang Qichao (梁启超) and other advocates. The effort ended when Empress Dowager Cixi (慈禧太后) regained control, confined the emperor and approved the execution of six reformers.
cards.note: 1898 is secure; “Hundred Days” conventionally refers to June–September. Proposed measures and enacted changes must be distinguished.

sections.title: Changing schools and government
sections.text: Reform proposals addressed education, administration and military effectiveness. Carrying them out required officials, money and support at court. Announcing a change in an imperial order could be much easier than making it work across the country. Reform also affected appointments and influence, so arguments about policy became struggles over who would direct government.

sections.title: Reform after the failure
sections.text: The defeat of the 1898 initiative did not end attempts to change the Qing state. After the Boxer crisis, the court itself supported major institutional reforms. Leaders who opposed one programme could adopt changes under different pressures. The Hundred Days remain a striking example of both the reach of an emperor’s orders and the limits of reform when support at court was fragile.

dateReview.note: 1898 is secure. The reform interval ran June–September; the Palace Museum gives fourth lunar month day 23 through eighth lunar month day 6, 103 days.

cards.catalogNote: 1898 is secure. The reform interval ran June–September; the Palace Museum gives fourth lunar month day 23 through eighth lunar month day 6, 103 days.
cards.significance: The reform attempt brought proposals for changing education and government to the centre of imperial politics. Its suppression showed how difficult it was to alter institutions without a durable coalition at court. Yet the underlying problems did not disappear, and the Qing later adopted major reforms of its own. The episode helps explain why reform and revolution developed side by side: some people continued to seek change through the monarchy, while others became less convinced that the throne could provide it.

significanceSources.label: Columbia University · The Qing reform edict of 1901

image.alt: A group of faculty members posed outside a building.
image.caption: Faculty and staff of the Imperial University of Peking, in a photograph published in 1901. The institution was one of the enduring products of the 1898 reform moment.

cards.name: Boxer Rebellion
cards.description: The Boxers were an anti-foreign and anti-Christian movement in northern China. They attacked missionaries and Chinese Christians. In 1900, support from the Qing court helped turn the crisis into war with foreign powers. An eight-nation force entered Beijing (北京) and ended the siege of the foreign legations.
cards.note: 1899–1901 covers the movement’s expansion and the final settlement. The main siege and foreign intervention took place in 1900; the movement’s roots were earlier.

sections.title: Violence within Chinese communities
sections.text: Foreign privileges and missionary protection of converts made local disputes part of larger conflicts over power. Drought and insecurity added to the tensions. Qing officials disagreed over how to respond: some supported the Boxers, while others suppressed them. Chinese Christians were major targets of attacks. The violence divided communities as well as involving foreign governments.

sections.title: Occupation and a costly settlement
sections.text: The court fled Beijing (北京). Foreign forces looted and carried out punitive expeditions. The Boxer Protocol of 1901 imposed a large payment and allowed foreign troops at strategic locations. The Qing survived, but its finances and security faced further restrictions. The dates 1899–1901 cover the movement’s expansion and settlement; the main siege and foreign intervention occurred in 1900.

sourceLabels.https://www.history.navy.mil/research/li: U.S. Naval History and Heritage Command · Boxer crisis

dateReview.note: 1900 is a valid focal marker for the siege and foreign intervention, not the movement's entire duration. Expansion preceded it in 1899 and settlement followed in 1901.

cards.catalogNote: 1900 is a valid focal marker for the siege and foreign intervention, not the movement's entire duration. Expansion preceded it in 1899 and settlement followed in 1901.
cards.significance: The Boxer crisis brought local hostility toward foreign influence, court politics and international military intervention into a disastrous collision. The settlement imposed heavy financial and security obligations on the Qing. It also sharpened the question of how the dynasty could protect the country when its own choices had helped bring foreign troops to the capital. The reforms that followed belong to this setting of lost authority and urgent repair, rather than a simple awakening after centuries without change.

significanceSources.label: National Army Museum · The Boxer Rebellion
Columbia University · Reform edict of 1901

image.alt: An illustration depicting fighting between Qing troops and foreign allied forces.
image.caption: An illustration of fighting between Qing troops and the foreign alliance. The Commons record does not identify the artist or date; this is a representation of the conflict, not a photograph.

cards.name: Xinhai (辛亥) Revolution
cards.description: The Wuchang (武昌) uprising in October 1911 helped trigger a series of provincial breaks with Qing rule. Revolutionary representatives elected Sun Yat-sen (孙中山) provisional president. The Republic of China began on 1 January 1912, and the Qing emperor abdicated on 12 February.
cards.note: 1911 marks the revolutionary outbreak. The republic began on 1 January 1912 and abdication followed on 12 February; the retained marker is not the exact end date of Qing sovereignty.

sections.title: How the monarchy ended
sections.text: Sun was abroad when the uprising began. Its spread depended on local soldiers, provincial decisions and negotiations with Yuan Shikai (袁世凯), whose forces were essential to the court. Sun later gave up the presidency in Yuan’s favour. The settlement joined revolutionary demands to the military power of a leader who had served the old regime.

sections.title: The problems facing the republic
sections.text: The end of the dynasty left armies, officials and regional interests in place. The new government had to decide how provinces would relate to the centre, how citizens would be represented and who could control military power. These questions remained unsettled. The revolution ended hereditary imperial rule and opened a new struggle over how China would be governed.

sourceLabels.https://history.state.gov/milestones/189: U.S. Office of the Historian · Revolution of 1911
sourceLabels.https://history.state.gov/historicaldocu: 1912 diplomatic record · Republic and imperial abdication

dateReview.note: 1911 marks the revolutionary outbreak. The republic began in January 1912 and imperial abdication occurred on 12 February 1912.

cards.catalogNote: 1911 marks the revolutionary outbreak. The republic began in January 1912 and imperial abdication occurred on 12 February 1912.
cards.significance: The revolution made replacing the dynasty a practical political outcome rather than only a programme debated by activists. Provincial withdrawals of support undermined the court, while negotiations helped determine the transfer to a republic. The monarchy’s collapse did not create an agreed national government with control over all armies. This gap between ending a regime and building a stable successor is central to the period that followed. It explains why 1911 and the founding of the republic are connected but distinct steps.

significanceSources.label: U.S. Office of the Historian · The Chinese Revolution of 1911

image.credit: Artist or photographer unidentified · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: Young men with equipment standing together at a port.
image.caption: Shanghai student expeditionary forces landing at Yantai in November 1911. The photograph records one local mobilization within the revolution, rather than a single nationwide event.

cards.name: Special Economic Zones
cards.description: Shenzhen (深圳), Zhuhai (珠海), Shantou (汕头) and Xiamen (厦门) became China’s first four special economic zones in 1980. Their special rules allowed experiments with investment and business. Shenzhen (深圳)’s location next to Hong Kong (香港) connected its growth to overseas money, trade and commercial experience.
cards.note: 1980 dates the first formal SEZ designations. Preparatory opening policies in Guangdong (广东) and Fujian (福建) began in 1979; a later wave created other types of development zones.

sections.title: Testing changes in selected places
sections.text: The zones gave officials a way to try economic policies within defined areas before extending them more widely. Investment depended on roads, transport, workers and local administration as well as rules for business. The results developed over time. Preparatory opening policies had begun in Guangdong (广东) and Fujian (福建) in 1979, before the formal designation of the four zones.

sections.title: Workers and growing cities
sections.text: Factories and construction attracted people into rapidly expanding urban areas. Their work helped turn investment into buildings, goods and trade. Migration also changed families’ living arrangements and access to jobs. The story of the zones includes both business growth and the everyday adjustments of the people who built and worked in them.

sourceLabels.https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated: World Bank · China’s special economic zones
sourceLabels.https://blogs.worldbank.org/en/eastasiap: World Bank · Forty years of reforms

dateReview.note: 26 August 1980: approval of Guangdong Special Economic Zone regulations, including Shenzhen. Preparatory policies date to 1979.

cards.catalogNote: 26 August 1980: approval of Guangdong Special Economic Zone regulations, including Shenzhen. Preparatory policies date to 1979.
cards.significance: The zones gave reform a place to be tested. Different rules for investment, trade and enterprise could be tried in selected locations before officials decided what to extend elsewhere. Their growth connected local labour and infrastructure to overseas capital and markets, helping reshape coastal cities and manufacturing. The broader lesson is how much China’s economic transformation relied on experiments and uneven regional change. A policy could spread because it appeared to work, without the whole country changing its rules at once.

significanceSources.label: World Bank · Building engines for growth and competitiveness in China

image.alt: A dense modern skyline of office towers and roads.
image.caption: The Futian district of Shenzhen, photographed in 2021. This later cityscape shows a long-term outcome of special-zone development, not the city’s appearance at the zone’s creation in 1980.

cards.name: Belt and Road Initiative
cards.description: The Belt and Road Initiative was launched in 2013 to promote connections, investment and cooperation across countries. It includes many separate projects and agreements, including transport corridors. Its name covers a broad programme whose scope and participants have changed over time.
cards.note: 2013 dates the initiative’s launch. Project membership and scope have changed; modelled benefits are scenarios rather than observed outcomes for every participating country.

sections.title: What infrastructure can change
sections.text: A railway or port can shorten journeys and lower the cost of moving goods. Those benefits also depend on border procedures, maintenance and connections to businesses that can use the route. A completed structure is only one part of the picture. The financing and operation of a project help determine whether it produces lasting gains.

sections.title: Different projects, different results
sections.text: Borrowers, lenders and contractors can receive different benefits and carry different risks. Debt, transparency and effects on local communities and the environment matter alongside construction costs. Each project needs to be assessed on its own evidence. Forecast benefits describe possible outcomes under stated assumptions; they do not establish what every participating country has already gained.

sourceLabels.https://documents.worldbank.org/en/publi: World Bank · Belt and Road Economics
sourceLabels.https://blogs.worldbank.org/en/eastasiap: World Bank · Managing Belt and Road risks

dateReview.note: The land and maritime initiatives were proposed in September and October 2013. This is the launch year, not the date of every project.

cards.catalogNote: The land and maritime initiatives were proposed in September and October 2013. This is the launch year, not the date of every project.
cards.significance: The initiative expanded China’s role in financing and building connections beyond its own borders. Roads, railways and ports can change where goods travel and which places gain access to markets. They also create obligations whose effects depend on project quality, debt terms and local decisions. Its historical importance lies in the scale of China’s outward economic involvement after decades of attracting foreign investment. Benefits and risks vary by country and project; the announcement alone cannot establish their eventual outcomes.

significanceSources.label: World Bank · Managing the risks of the Belt and Road

image.alt: A container terminal with cranes and rows of shipping containers.
image.caption: Yangshan port near Shanghai, photographed before the Belt and Road Initiative. It is contextual evidence for the maritime trade infrastructure on which later connectivity policies built, not a Belt and Road project inaugurated in 2013.

cards.name: Xi Jinping (习近平) assumes party leadership
cards.description: Xi Jinping (习近平) became Communist Party general secretary in November 2012 and state president in March 2013. These are different offices. Subsequent changes increased the emphasis on centralized party leadership; the 2018 constitutional amendment removed the two-term limit for the state presidency.
cards.note: 2012 is an accession date, not a single moment when consolidation was complete. The presidency began in 2013; the term-limit change occurred in 2018. This is a historical account of those changes.

sections.title: Titles do not carry equal power
sections.text: Political authority rests on party and military leadership as well as the formal presidency. Describing 2018 simply as the removal of a limit on all Chinese leadership would therefore misstate the institutions involved. The change mattered because it removed a particular succession constraint and altered expectations, not because it created presidential government from nothing.

sections.title: Centralization as a governing choice
sections.text: Central leadership can seek tighter coordination and discipline while also making policy correction depend more heavily on signals from the top. This is an analytical tradeoff rather than a prediction of inevitable outcomes. The card treats 2012 as the beginning of a leadership phase and 2018 as a documented institutional change, without projecting later developments into the original accession.

sourceLabels.https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_pr: Congressional Research Service · China’s 2018 constitutional changes

dateReview.note: 15 November 2012 dates appointment as party general secretary. Political consolidation was a subsequent process, not a completed event that year.

cards.catalogNote: 15 November 2012 dates appointment as party general secretary. Political consolidation was a subsequent process, not a completed event that year.
cards.significance: Xi Jinping (习近平)’s rise marks the beginning of a leadership period associated with a stronger role for the Communist Party across government and society. Later institutional changes concentrated authority and altered arrangements that had developed after Mao. The distinction matters because taking office in 2012 did not enact every later policy at once. Placed in the longer history of the People’s Republic, this leadership transition opens a new chapter in the recurring question of how power is distributed within the party and the state.

significanceSources.label: Congressional Research Service · China’s Communist Party absorbs more of the state

image.credit: White House photo by Eric Draper · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: Xi Jinping and George W. Bush greeting each other.
image.caption: Xi Jinping, then vice-president, with George W. Bush in August 2008. The photograph predates Xi’s accession to the party leadership in 2012.

cards.name: Modern China
cards.description: This atlas begins its Modern China section in 1912, when the Republic of China was established and Qing rule ended. The period includes wars, revolutions and far-reaching changes to work and family life. The Republic and the People’s Republic have distinct government histories.
cards.note: 1912 is a convenient exhibition boundary. Intellectual, economic and political roots extend into the Qing; the present-day endpoint does not forecast an outcome.

sections.title: Changes beyond the capital
sections.text: Schools, factories, newspapers and migration brought politics into new parts of everyday life. Parties and governments organized people through campaigns and offices that reached deep into society. A village family, a factory worker and a refugee could experience the same turning point very differently. Following their circumstances helps make sense of a history often told through leaders and wars.

sections.title: Different paths through the twentieth century
sections.text: Mainland China, Taiwan (台湾) and Hong Kong (香港) experienced different combinations of political change and economic growth. Their histories also remained connected through trade, migration and conflict. The entries separate particular events from changes that developed over decades. The 1912 boundary is a choice for this atlas; many developments in the section had roots in the Qing period.

sourceLabels.https://history.state.gov/countries/chin: U.S. Office of the Historian · Recognition and diplomatic relations
sourceLabels.https://blogs.worldbank.org/en/eastasiap: World Bank · Forty years of reforms
sourceLabels.https://1997-2001.state.gov/background_n: U.S. State Department · Taiwan historical background (2000)

dateReview.note: 1912–2026 is an editorial exhibition frame. Modern China has no universally agreed beginning; 2026 is a display horizon.

cards.catalogNote: 1912–2026 is an editorial exhibition frame. Modern China has no universally agreed beginning; 2026 is a display horizon.
cards.significance: Beginning this section with the republic highlights the end of hereditary imperial rule and the search for a different basis of national government. That search took competing forms through revolution, war, party rule and economic reform. There was no single path shared equally by every region or community. Following these changes together helps a beginner see how present institutions emerged from difficult choices and conflicts, rather than appearing fully formed when one government replaced another. The section boundary is a reading guide, not a claim that every aspect of life changed in 1912.

significanceSources.label: U.S. Office of the Historian · China and changes of government
Office of the President, ROC · Historical introduction

image.alt: Sun Yat-sen and Li Yuanhong standing together in formal dress.
image.caption: Sun Yat-sen and Li Yuanhong at Wuchang in April 1912. Their encounter belongs to the early republic’s effort to convert revolutionary coalitions into a functioning state.

cards.name: May Fourth Movement
cards.description: On 4 May 1919, students protested in Beijing (北京) against the Versailles peace settlement’s treatment of German rights in Shandong (山东) and the actions of Chinese officials. Boycotts, strikes and public organizing spread the movement beyond the campuses. The name May Fourth also came to describe wider cultural debates.
cards.note: 4 May 1919 dates the protest. “May Fourth” also names a broader cultural movement whose boundaries vary by historian.

sections.title: From students to a wider movement
sections.text: The peace settlement raised a direct question about who could decide the fate of territory and foreign privileges in China. Students linked anger over diplomacy with criticism of their own government. Workers and merchants also took part. They shared some concerns while bringing different interests and experiences to the movement.

sections.title: Debating China’s future
sections.text: Writers and activists argued over education, family authority and the language of literature. They explored liberalism, anarchism, Marxism and other ideas. These discussions had begun before the May demonstrations and continued afterwards. The movement had several possible directions; its participants did not all agree on the changes China needed or how to bring them about.

sourceLabels.https://afe.easia.columbia.edu/special/c: Columbia Asia for Educators · May Fourth
sourceLabels.https://www.marxists.org/archive/lu-xun/: Lu Xun · A Madman’s Diary (translated primary text)

dateReview.note: 4 May 1919 dates the Beijing protest; the wider movement has broader boundaries.

cards.catalogNote: 4 May 1919 dates the Beijing protest; the wider movement has broader boundaries.
cards.significance: May Fourth connected anger over China’s treatment abroad with demands to change society at home. Students, writers, merchants and workers helped make public protest and cultural debate part of national politics. Arguments over language, family authority, science and political organization reached well beyond one demonstration. This matters because new ideas could now circulate through journals and education and then become programmes for action. The movement influenced several political directions, so its importance cannot be reduced to preparing the way for only one later party.

significanceSources.label: Columbia University · The May Fourth Movement

image.credit: Artist or photographer unidentified · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: A large crowd of students gathered before a monumental gate.
image.caption: Student demonstrators in Beijing on 4 May 1919. The photograph documents a public mobilization that expanded into a wider argument over sovereignty, language, and social authority.

cards.name: Long March
cards.description: During 1934–1936, Communist armies left threatened bases and undertook a series of difficult retreats. The best-known force departed Jiangxi in 1934 and reached northern Shaanxi (陕西) in 1935. Heavy losses marked the journeys that later became known collectively as the Long March.
cards.note: 1934–1936 includes the principal Communist army retreats; 1934–1935 usually refers to the First Front Army. Some influential accounts rely substantially on participants’ later recollections.

sections.title: Retreat under military pressure
sections.text: The armies followed different routes as they tried to escape attacks and find places to regroup. Food, terrain, hostile forces and relations with local communities affected their chances of survival. The march was a struggle whose outcome remained uncertain. Treating it as a single journey can hide the different experiences of the forces involved.

sections.title: A powerful story of survival
sections.text: The Long March later became central to Communist accounts of the revolution. Poems and recollections helped turn the retreats into a story of endurance and leadership. Mao’s position strengthened over time, but disputes within the movement continued during the journeys. The broad dates 1934–1936 include several principal army retreats; 1934–1935 usually refers to the best-known column.

sourceLabels.https://afe.easia.columbia.edu/special/c: Columbia · Snow and Mao on the Long March
Columbia · Leaders of the People’s Republic

dateReview.note: 1934 is the beginning anchor. October 1934–October 1936 covers multiple Red Army retreats; 1934–1935 covers the best-known First Front Army route.

cards.catalogNote: 1934 is the beginning anchor. October 1934–October 1936 covers multiple Red Army retreats; 1934–1935 covers the best-known First Front Army route.
cards.significance: The retreat preserved part of the Communist movement after the loss of its southern bases, but at immense human cost. Survivors regrouped in the northwest, where the party could rebuild. The journey also became a powerful story of endurance used to explain and justify later leadership. It therefore matters in two ways: as a military escape that kept a political organization alive, and as a remembered experience that shaped its identity. Survival on the march did not make eventual victory certain.

significanceSources.label: Columbia University · Mao and the Long March

image.alt: A chain suspension bridge crossing a steep-sided river gorge.
image.caption: Luding Bridge, photographed in 2006. The surviving crossing is associated with the Long March; the modern view is not a record of the 1935 fighting.

cards.name: Death of Mao Zedong (毛泽东)
cards.description: Mao Zedong (毛泽东) died on 9 September 1976. Within a month, Hua Guofeng (华国锋) and his allies arrested the Gang of Four. These events changed the balance of power at the top of the Communist Party. The economic reforms associated with 1978 still lay ahead.
cards.note: 1976 marks Mao’s death and the succession crisis. The policy shift conventionally associated with 1978 developed afterwards.

sections.title: Who would lead next?
sections.text: Mao had exercised exceptional personal authority. His successors had to decide which policies and officials to retain while presenting themselves as legitimate heirs to the revolution. Arresting the Gang of Four resolved an immediate struggle for power. It did not settle the direction of economic policy or establish lasting agreement about how the leadership should work.

sections.title: A change that took time
sections.text: Public mourning emphasized continuity with Mao’s era, while later leaders changed many of its policies. Decisions about reform developed through further arguments and experiments. Mao’s death was a major turning point, but the policies of the following years did not emerge all at once. The 1976 succession crisis and the 1978 shift toward reform are separate milestones.

sourceLabels.https://afe.easia.columbia.edu/special/c: Columbia · Leaders of the People’s Republic

dateReview.note: Mao died on 9 September 1976.

cards.catalogNote: Mao died on 9 September 1976.
cards.significance: Mao’s death removed the leader whose personal authority had shaped decades of revolution and political campaigns. It opened a struggle over who would govern and which policies would continue. The economic reforms associated with the following years emerged from that struggle and later decisions; they were not an automatic consequence of his death. The moment matters because it separates the end of a dominant leader’s rule from the slower reworking of the institutions and policies he left behind.

significanceSources.label: Chinese Posters · After Mao

image.alt: Tiananmen gate displaying a mourning portrait and banners.
image.caption: Tiananmen in September 1976, shortly after the official mourning ceremony for Mao. The photograph records public commemoration during a moment of uncertain succession.

cards.name: Tiananmen (天安门) protests and crackdown
cards.description: In 1989, students, workers and other residents joined protests in Beijing (北京) and other Chinese cities. Their demands included action against corruption and greater government accountability. On the night of 3–4 June, troops used lethal force in Beijing (北京). Arrests and repression followed the suppression of the movement.
cards.note: 1989 covers the protests and suppression. Casualty totals remain disputed; uncertainty over totals does not imply uncertainty that troops killed civilians.

sections.title: People with different demands
sections.text: Participants brought concerns about rising prices, privilege, representation and political reform. Students and workers did not always share the same priorities. Their involvement made the protests broader than a single campus movement. Economic and political questions overlapped as people called for changes in the way officials exercised power.

sections.title: The crackdown beyond the square
sections.text: Much of the killing occurred on streets approaching Tiananmen (天安门) Square. The familiar name therefore covers events across a wider area of Beijing (北京). Contemporary reports document troops killing civilians, although the full number and identities of the victims remain uncertain. Disagreement over casualty totals does not cast doubt on the fact of the killings. The repression also continued through arrests after the military operation.

sourceLabels.https://nsarchive2.gwu.edu/NSAEBB/NSAEBB: National Security Archive · Tiananmen: declassified history
sourceLabels.https://history.state.gov/milestones/198: U.S. Office of the Historian · Tiananmen, 1989

dateReview.note: 1989 covers the protest movement. The Beijing military crackdown occurred on the night of 3–4 June.

cards.catalogNote: 1989 covers the protest movement. The Beijing military crackdown occurred on the night of 3–4 June.
cards.significance: The protests exposed demands for accountability and political change during a period of rapid economic reform. The military crackdown made clear the leadership’s willingness to use force to preserve party control. It also damaged relations with other countries and left lasting trauma for those affected. In the longer arc, the episode helps explain why expanding markets did not necessarily produce greater political freedom. Subsequent economic growth took place alongside continuing restrictions on public discussion and commemoration of the crackdown.

significanceSources.label: U.S. Office of the Historian · Tiananmen Square, 1989
National Security Archive · Documents on Tiananmen
