sections.text: A court on useful routes could gain influence by managing connections and exchange. Trade and diplomatic payments operated together. Jingnan’s importance came partly from its position between other states, rather than from commanding a vast territory or the largest army.

sections.title: Room to govern
sections.text: Accepting another ruler’s titles and making payments could coexist with real control at home. Jingnan’s leaders had limited bargaining power, but enough to preserve a local court for a time. Their independence rested on a changing set of relationships rather than complete freedom from outside pressure.

sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs: Hugh Clark · Southern kingdoms between Tang and Song
sourceLabels.https://www.ocha-festival.jp/archive/eng: International Conference on O-CHA · Tea trade in the tenth century

dateReview.note: Existing range confirmed by Cambridge History of China, volume 5 introduction table; starts use state-formation milestones.

cards.catalogNote: Existing range confirmed by Cambridge History of China, volume 5 introduction table; starts use state-formation milestones.
cards.significance: Jingnan's small size makes its survival instructive. A court situated between stronger neighbours could gain room to act by managing routes, payments and diplomatic recognition. Its history shows that political importance did not always match territorial extent. In the broader transition from Tang to Song, states like this helped connect regions that larger dynasties claimed but did not yet control. Their rulers' choices reveal a world of negotiated dependence, where accepting another court's titles could coexist with practical authority at home.

significanceSources.label: International Conference on O-CHA · Tea trade in the tenth century
Hugh Clark · Southern kingdoms between Tang and Song

image.alt: A modern historical map of Later Jin and neighboring kingdoms.
image.caption: A modern reconstruction of Later Jin and neighboring states in 939. The map shows political coexistence rather than a single dynasty ruling the whole region. Southern kingdoms appear as independent polities, not provinces of Later Jin.

cards.name: Later Shu
cards.description: Meng Zhixiang (孟知祥) founded Later Shu in Sichuan (四川) in 934, turning a governorship under Later Tang into an independent court. Under Meng Chang (孟昶), the state sustained regional government and literary life until Song conquered it in 965.
cards.note: 934–965 dates Later Shu; it followed the Later Tang occupation after Former Shu’s fall in 925.

sections.title: An imperial office becomes a throne
sections.text: When northern supervision weakened, a regional commander could use his existing position to seek greater independence. Later Shu grew from offices and resources already established in Sichuan (四川). The authorities these institutions answered to changed, while much of the machinery of local government continued.

sections.title: Two Shu dynasties
sections.text: Later Shu ruled much of the same region as Wang Jian (王建)’s Former Shu, but belonged to a different family. Regional culture and institutions could survive a change of dynasty and find new patrons. The shared name describes a connection to Sichuan (四川), not the return of the earlier ruling house.

sourceLabels.https://assets.cambridge.org/97805218/12: Cambridge History of China · Tenth-century chronology
sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs: Hugh Clark · Southern kingdoms between Tang and Song

dateReview.note: 934–965 agrees with Jordan's university-hosted reign table.

cards.catalogNote: 934–965 agrees with Jordan's university-hosted reign table.
cards.significance: Later Shu reveals the durability of Sichuan (四川) as a regional centre across conquest and changes of ruling family. Institutions and resources established under one authority could support another when northern control weakened. Its relationship to Former Shu is therefore geographical and institutional rather than a simple restoration of the same house. This distinction matters throughout Chinese history: continuity in local society can be stronger than continuity at the throne, and a new dynasty may depend on arrangements it did not create.

significanceSources.label: Cambridge History of China · Tenth-century chronology
Hugh Clark · Southern kingdoms between Tang and Song

image.alt: The entrance and grounds of a royal tomb complex.
image.caption: The Yongling tomb of Wang Jian, founder of Former Shu, photographed in 2010. The site provides a specific Chengdu setting for the kingdom’s royal culture. The tomb belongs to the earlier Former Shu dynasty; it supplies context for Chengdu’s inherited royal landscape, not a tomb of Later Shu’s rulers.

cards.name: Southern Tang
cards.description: Southern Tang inherited Wu’s regional government in 937. Its rulers claimed imperial standing and expanded into neighbouring territory before losing ground to northern powers. The last ruler, Li Yu (李煜), is especially remembered for his poetry.
cards.note: 937–975 follows the conquest-year convention. Some chronologies use 976 because of dating conventions.

sections.title: Claiming the Tang inheritance
sections.text: The dynasty used ancestry claims and the Tang name to present its rule as legitimate. That connection was politically constructed and argued over. The name alone does not prove a straightforward family line from the earlier Tang emperors.

sections.title: A court beyond its poems
sections.text: Li Yu (李煜)’s literary fame is one part of the state’s history. Its rulers also maintained armies, collected income and negotiated with rivals. Poetry and government existed in the same court, but literary achievement does not by itself explain military defeat. Southern Tang’s end came through a struggle with stronger northern power.

sourceLabels.https://fass.ubd.edu.bn/staff/docs/JK/ha: Johannes Kurz · Han Xizai and Southern Tang
sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs: Hugh Clark · Southern kingdoms between Tang and Song

dateReview.note: 937–975 agrees with Jordan's university-hosted reign table.

cards.catalogNote: 937–975 agrees with Jordan's university-hosted reign table.
cards.significance: Southern Tang joined political ambition to the cultural prestige of the Tang name, while its court supported a literary life remembered long after military defeat. Li Yu (李煜)'s poetry is part of that survival, but the state also rested on the lower Yangtze (长江)'s resources and institutions inherited from Yang Wu. Its history connects regional courts to the culture and economy later incorporated into Song. Conquest changed who ruled these resources; it did not mean that their value or traditions began with the conqueror.

significanceSources.label: Johannes Kurz · Han Xizai and Southern Tang
Princeton University Art Museum · Southern Tang art

image.credit: Русский: Чжоу Вэньцзюй English: Zhou Wenju (10th century) · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: Courtly figures gathered around a board game.
image.caption: A tenth-century painting of weiqi players attributed to Zhou Wenju. Associated with Southern Tang court culture, it shows elite sociability rather than a specific political meeting. The painting is associated with Southern Tang, which succeeded Yang Wu; it does not portray an identified Yang Wu court gathering.

cards.name: Northern Han
cards.description: Northern Han preserved a Liu-family court in Shanxi (山西) after Later Han fell in 951. It relied on Liao support while claiming imperial authority of its own. Song conquered it in 979.
cards.note: 951–979 dates Northern Han, distinct from the Earlier Han empire and the short Later Han dynasty.

sections.title: A stronger ally
sections.text: Liao ties offered protection and recognition, while limiting the court’s choices. Depending on an ally did not mean giving up every claim to authority at home. Northern Han’s rulers combined an imperial title with the practical need for support from a larger neighbour.

sections.title: The northern kingdom
sections.text: Despite its location, Northern Han is traditionally counted among the Ten Kingdoms. It also survived beyond Song’s foundation in 960. Its history helps explain why neither the name Ten Kingdoms nor the end of the Five Dynasties describes a single tidy boundary in place or time.

sourceLabels.https://assets.cambridge.org/97805218/12: Cambridge History of China · Tenth-century chronology
sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs: Hugh Clark · Southern kingdoms between Tang and Song

dateReview.note: 951–979 agrees with Jordan's university-hosted reign table.

cards.catalogNote: 951–979 agrees with Jordan's university-hosted reign table.
cards.significance: Northern Han's survival after Song's foundation shows why 960 did not instantly restore a united realm. Support from Liao helped a smaller court resist a stronger neighbour, linking the struggle for northern territory to a wider balance of power. Its eventual conquest marked a further stage in Song consolidation. The distinction is useful beyond this one kingdom: founding a dynasty, eliminating rival claimants and securing a frontier are different tasks, and success at one does not automatically complete the others.

significanceSources.label: Cambridge History of China · Tenth-century chronology

image.alt: A modern historical map of Later Zhou and neighboring kingdoms.
image.caption: A modern reconstruction of Later Zhou and its neighbors in 951. Northern Han appears as a separate state; this is a retrospective map with approximate boundaries.

cards.name: Ten Kingdoms
cards.description: The Ten Kingdoms were regional states around the transition from Tang to Song. They began and ended at different times and did not all exist together. Northern Han, despite the common association of these kingdoms with the south, lay in the north.
cards.note: 902–979 is a broad span for the regional kingdoms, extending beyond the northern Five Dynasties period of 907–960.

sections.title: Life beyond the northern courts
sections.text: Some kingdoms lasted much longer than the rapidly changing Five Dynasties in the north. Their governments supported farming, sea trade, religious institutions and cultural life. Warfare mattered, but its effects differed across regions; political division did not make every place equally unstable.

sections.title: Different paths to Song rule
sections.text: The states varied in size and in their relationships with stronger neighbours. Some were conquered, while others negotiated submission. Each ruling house relied on its own combination of local resources, military support and diplomacy. Song reunification brought these different regional histories together over time.

sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs: Hugh Clark · Southern kingdoms between Tang and Song
sourceLabels.https://assets.cambridge.org/97805218/12: Cambridge History of China · Tenth-century chronology

dateReview.note: 902–979 agrees with Jordan's university-hosted reign table.

cards.catalogNote: 902–979 agrees with Jordan's university-hosted reign table.
cards.significance: The Ten Kingdoms reveal how much happened outside the rapidly changing northern courts. Regional governments sustained commerce, religious communities and cultural patronage, while making different choices about war and recognition. Song later incorporated many of these resources rather than creating them afresh. This changes the meaning of political division: it could bring destructive conflict while also leaving space for durable regional institutions. The history of reunification becomes clearer when the societies being joined are treated as active participants in the process.

significanceSources.label: Hugh Clark · Southern kingdoms between Tang and Song

image.credit: Artist or photographer unidentified · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: Women gathered inside a palace in a vertical painting.
image.caption: Palace Banquet, a painting assigned to the tenth-century Five Dynasties–early Song milieu, in the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Court culture continued across rapid political changes.

cards.name: Grand Canal
cards.description: Emperor Yang (隋炀帝) joined and enlarged older waterways into a vast transport network. Work on the Tongji Canal began in 605, and the Jiangnan (江南) extension was completed in 610. These projects connected regional routes around Luoyang (洛阳) rather than creating one entirely new canal.

sections.title: Grain for capitals and armies
sections.text: Sui had reunited north and south in 589. The canals helped make that territory governable by carrying southern grain toward northern political centres. A northern branch supplied frontier armies. Harvests collected far from the court could now feed officials and soldiers elsewhere, linking local production to the needs of a much larger empire.

sections.title: The labour behind the waterway
sections.text: Construction demanded enormous amounts of labour. These burdens helped give Emperor Yang (隋炀帝) a reputation for destructive excess. Yet Tang and later dynasties continued to benefit from the network. Its lasting usefulness and its immediate human cost belong to the same story: generations of rulers inherited infrastructure that people under Sui had been compelled to build.

cards.note: 605–610 marks Emperor Yang (隋炀帝)’s principal expansion. Earlier canals, including work under Emperor Wen (隋文帝), preceded it; later dynasties changed the routes. The modern Beijing (北京)–Hangzhou (杭州) alignment should not be projected unchanged onto the Sui network.

dateReview.note: 605–610 marks Sui expansion and connection of earlier waterways; it is not the origin of all Chinese canals.

searchAliases: Sui builds the Grand Canal network
cards.significance: The canal helped make a large empire governable by moving bulky supplies between regions, linking political centres to the people and production that sustained them. Its continuing maintenance under later dynasties mattered as much as the original construction. This connection grew especially important as southern economic resources supported courts farther north. The canal's history therefore explains a recurring feature of Chinese government: holding territory required transport and administration across long distances, built through labour demands that could themselves become sources of hardship.

significanceSources.label: UNESCO World Heritage Centre

image.alt: Tour boats on a canal in Suzhou, alongside waterside buildings.
image.caption: Canal boats in Suzhou, photographed in 2018. This modern view illustrates the enduring waterway landscape, not the appearance or exact route of the Sui canal.

cards.name: Bi Sheng (毕升)’s movable type
cards.description: Bi Sheng (毕升) made individual clay characters that could be arranged for printing and used again. Shen Kuo (沈括) described this work during the Qingli period, 1041–1048. His account preserves both Bi Sheng (毕升)’s name and the practical details of the method.
cards.note: 1041–1048 is the Qingli reign-period range given for the work, not a proven seven-year development project. Movable type did not immediately replace woodblock printing.

sections.title: Reusable characters or a whole page
sections.text: Movable characters could be rearranged for different texts, but setting them took work. Woodblocks preserved a complete page for reprinting and could combine writing with images. Both methods remained useful because different printing jobs had different costs. Reusability did not make movable type the best choice for every book.

sections.title: A craftsman in a scholar’s book
sections.text: Much of what we know about Bi Sheng (毕升) comes through Shen Kuo (沈括). By recording the materials and procedure, Shen preserved knowledge that might otherwise have remained within a workshop. The account tells us that this technique was being practised in the stated period; it does not supply a precise day when movable type was first invented.

sourceLabels.https://scalar.usc.edu/works/chinese-rar: University of Southern California · Chinese printing techniques

dateReview.note: 1041–1048 is the attestation window for Bi Sheng's work, not a securely dated seven-year project. Preserve the range and make uncertainty visible.

cards.significance: Bi Sheng (毕升)'s work matters because it shows printers experimenting with how to reproduce and rearrange written knowledge. Its historical importance does not depend on imagining an immediate replacement of woodblocks: different methods suited different jobs, and block printing remained highly effective. The larger change was the growth of a society in which books could circulate more widely and support study, religion and commerce. Movable type belongs within that continuing development of production methods, rather than explaining the whole expansion of learning by itself.

significanceSources.label: University of Southern California · Chinese printing techniques

cards.pinyin: bì shēng yǔ huó zì yìn shuā

image.credit: Anonymous Tang printers; commissioned by Wang Jie · British Library
image.alt: A printed Buddhist assembly above columns of Chinese text.
image.caption: The frontispiece of the Diamond Sutra dated 868, now in the British Library. Its survival makes the relationship between devotion, sponsorship, and woodblock reproduction unusually concrete. The 868 object uses woodblock printing; it must not be mistaken for a surviving example of Bi Sheng’s later movable type.

cards.name: Along the River During Qingming
cards.description: Zhang Zeduan (张择端)’s Northern Song handscroll moves from a rural approach into a busy riverfront and city. Boats, workers, shops and customers fill its scenes. The original survives in the Palace Museum in Beijing (北京).
cards.note: Early twelfth century, approximately 1100–1127; the exact production year is not secure. The conventional English title does not settle every scholarly interpretation of “Qingming.”

sections.title: Follow the river
sections.text: Water transport brings supplies toward the city, while streets connect people doing different kinds of work. At the bridge, interacting tasks and hazards draw the viewer into the activity. The city’s prosperity appears through people moving goods and serving customers, as well as through its buildings.

sections.title: What a painting can show
sections.text: The artist selected and arranged these scenes. They offer a rich view of urban life, but cannot serve as a complete record of Kaifeng (开封)’s population or economy. Later artists made their own versions for different audiences and purposes. Those copies reveal the worlds in which they were produced, so they should be distinguished from the Northern Song original.

sourceLabels.https://www.dpm.org.cn/collection/paint/: Palace Museum · Zhang Zeduan’s Qingming scroll
sourceLabels.https://afe.easia.columbia.edu/songdynas: Columbia University · Two versions of the Qingming scroll

dateReview.note: Museums support early twelfth century. 1100–1127 is an approximate display envelope, not two independently attested production dates.

cards.significance: The scroll makes the workings of a city visible in a history often dominated by emperors and battles. Boats, shops, transport and crowds direct attention to the ordinary coordination that supported urban prosperity. Comparing its details with other evidence helps connect Song commercial growth to people performing particular jobs. Its later versions also show how generations revisited an admired urban past. The image is carefully composed, but that does not diminish its value as evidence for what city life meant to artists and patrons.

significanceSources.label: Columbia University · Two versions of the Qingming scroll

image.alt: Busy streets, shops, boats, and a city gate in a scroll painting.
image.caption: A section of Along the River During the Qingming Festival, attributed to Zhang Zeduan. Its carefully organized urban world is an artistic representation, not an unfiltered census of Northern Song life.

cards.name: China and the Manila Silver Trade
cards.description: Spanish Manila became a major trading meeting point after its establishment in 1571. Chinese merchants brought silk and ceramics, while silver arrived across the Pacific from the Americas. The port connected existing Asian trade with a growing route across two oceans.
cards.note: 1571 marks Spanish establishment at Manila. The route’s development was gradual, and silver also reached China through other channels, including Japan.

sections.title: Why silver mattered
sections.text: Silver was important in Chinese trade and tax payments. Merchants therefore had strong reasons to obtain it. Pacific shipping linked American mines with Asian markets, alongside other supplies such as Japanese silver. The route connected miners, sailors, traders and households across distant societies. Some of the labour supporting those exchanges was coerced.

sections.title: Wealth and changing prices
sections.text: More silver could make trade easier, but changes in its value also affected people who earned money in one form and paid taxes in another. The benefits of growing commerce were uneven. Silver supplies formed one part of the pressures on the later Ming economy. Military spending, taxation, harvests and rebellion also mattered to the dynasty’s final crisis.

sourceLabels.https://blogs.loc.gov/international-coll: Library of Congress · Founding of Manila
sourceLabels.https://afe.easia.columbia.edu/qing/econ: Columbia University · Silver and the wider Chinese economy

dateReview.note: 1571 correctly marks Spanish establishment in Manila; the trade itself developed gradually and had earlier regional foundations.

searchAliases: China and the Manila Silver Trade
cards.significance: The silver trade connected Chinese demand for money with mines and markets across the Pacific. Merchants exchanged Chinese goods for silver that could circulate through trade and tax payments at home. This makes the Ming economy part of a wider world long before nineteenth-century treaty ports. It also shows how distant changes could matter to Chinese households: when obligations were payable in silver, access to that metal and its value affected the real burden of payment.

significanceSources.label: Columbia University · China and the world economy

cards.pinyin: mǎ ní lā yǔ bái yín mào yì

image.alt: A silver coin stamped with several small Chinese marks.
image.caption: A Mexican Spanish dollar dated 1796, bearing Chinese merchant chop marks. This later coin illustrates the long-lived silver trade, not a coin documented on the first Manila galleon.

cards.name: Dream of the Red Chamber
cards.description: Dream of the Red Chamber follows the fortunes of an elite household, bringing love, marriage, property and family duty into one story. Cao Xueqin (曹雪芹)’s work circulated in manuscripts before the Cheng-Gao edition printed a 120-chapter version in 1791.
cards.note: 1791 is a printing milestone, not the date of composition. The last forty chapters are not attributed unreservedly to Cao Xueqin (曹雪芹).

sections.title: Life inside a wealthy household
sections.text: The family’s luxurious world depends on servants, careful management and connections outside the home. Personal attachments meet the demands of rank and obligation. Through these relationships, the novel explores the insecurity beneath wealth and status. Its fictional household offers a way into questions about Qing society, although it cannot stand for the experience of every family.

sections.title: How the book reached readers
sections.text: Manuscripts, editors and printers shaped the versions that readers encountered. The authorship of the final forty chapters remains disputed, so the printed edition should not be described as Cao’s unchanged original. The date 1791 marks a major stage in publication. The story and its earlier manuscript versions had developed before that printing milestone.

sourceLabels.https://open.lib.umn.edu/redchamber/part: University of Minnesota · Text of Dream of the Red Chamber
sourceLabels.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dream_of_t: Wikipedia · Dream of the Red Chamber

dateReview.note: 1791 is the publication milestone; earlier manuscript circulation and the disputed last forty chapters are correctly distinguished.

searchAliases: Dream of the Red Chamber in print
cards.significance: The novel makes the household a place from which to understand a whole social order. Affection, marriage, servants, money and official connections shape the fortunes of its characters, showing how private lives depended on family hierarchy and public power. For a beginner, that offers something a list of emperors cannot: a sense of the pressures inside elite society and the voices of women within it. Its literary achievement lies in turning those relationships into a complex human world, rather than simply illustrating a dynasty’s decline.

significanceSources.label: University of Minnesota · Dream of the Red Chamber

cards.pinyin: hóng lóu mèng shǒu cì kān yìn

image.alt: A garden scene with figures from a Chinese novel.
image.caption: Sun Wen’s nineteenth-century illustration of Dream of the Red Chamber. It belongs to the novel’s later reception, not the original 1791 printed edition.

cards.name: Great Leap Forward
cards.description: The Great Leap Forward began in 1958 with demands for rapid growth in farming and industry. Communes, mass campaigns and ambitious targets reorganized work. The policies contributed to a devastating famine. Inflated reports and pressure to meet state demands made shortages harder to recognize and correct.
cards.note: 1958–1962 covers the campaign and famine crisis. Narrower campaign and famine chronologies differ. Mortality estimates vary substantially; no falsely precise total is supplied.

sections.title: When harvest reports became dangerous
sections.text: Officials faced pressure to report success. Exaggerated harvest figures could lead the state to demand more grain than villages could spare. People responsible for reporting problems also faced political risks. These pressures allowed serious mistakes to continue and made it harder for those losing access to food to obtain help.

sections.title: Promises and hunger
sections.text: Campaign posters showed huge harvests and plentiful food. They reveal what the campaign promised, rather than what farms actually produced. Hunger varied between places and social groups, depending partly on access to food and the decisions of officials. The dates 1958–1962 cover the campaign and famine crisis. Estimates of deaths vary substantially, and no precise total is asserted here.

sourceLabels.https://afe.easia.columbia.edu/special/c: Columbia · Leaders of the People’s Republic

dateReview.note: 1958 is the campaign launch. The displayed 1958–1962 frame includes the famine crisis and retreat from the campaign; Chinese Posters uses 1958–1961 for the campaign. These are different scope conventions.

cards.significance: The Great Leap Forward shows how a drive for rapid transformation could become catastrophic when political pressure displaced reliable information and practical limits. Collectivization, production demands and food procurement contributed to famine on an enormous scale. The disaster matters for understanding both the reach of the new state and the dangers of policies that made reporting failure difficult. Later changes in rural organization took place against this experience, although they emerged through further struggles rather than an immediate, agreed rejection of collective farming.

significanceSources.label: Chinese Posters · The Great Leap Forward

image.credit: Artist or photographer unidentified · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: People working around small furnaces in a rural setting.
image.caption: Backyard furnaces photographed in 1958. The mobilization for steel production made the Great Leap’s production ambitions visible, but the photograph cannot by itself measure its costs or famine mortality.

cards.name: Cultural Revolution
cards.description: Mao launched the Cultural Revolution in 1966, calling for attacks on supposed enemies in the Communist Party and society. Red Guards, rival factions and later military intervention disrupted government and everyday life. Persecution, violence and damaged education marked the decade, which conventionally ends in 1976.
cards.note: 1966–1976 is a conventional frame, not a claim that the same institutions or intensity of violence prevailed everywhere for ten years.

sections.title: Rebellion in Mao’s name
sections.text: Participants challenged officials while claiming support from Mao. Rival groups fought over who truly represented the revolution. The ability to attack authority did not give people unrestricted political freedom. Institutions were disrupted and authority was later reimposed, including through military intervention. The forms and intensity of conflict changed over the decade.

sections.title: Lives shaped by political campaigns
sections.text: Schooling was interrupted, families were separated and people were forced to move. Posters, performances and public rituals made political demands part of daily life. These official images show the behaviour authorities promoted, but they cannot tell us what every person believed. Mao’s death and the arrest of the Gang of Four in 1976 mark the conventional end of this period.

sourceLabels.https://mao-static.kdl.kcl.ac.uk/object-: King’s College London · Mao Era in Objects: posters

dateReview.note: 1966–1976 is the conventional decade: launch in 1966, Mao’s death and arrest of the Gang of Four in 1976.

cards.significance: The Cultural Revolution brought struggles over political loyalty into schools, workplaces and families, disrupting institutions that the Communist government itself had built. Violence and persecution left consequences that lasted beyond the campaign’s formal end. Its importance is therefore both institutional and personal: later leaders had to rebuild systems of education and administration, while survivors carried memories that could not be repaired by a policy announcement. Cultural production during these years also shaped a generation, even as many older forms of learning and expression were attacked.

significanceSources.label: Columbia University · Mao and the People’s Republic
Harvard Fairbank Center · Cultural Revolution culture

image.alt: Large handwritten posters covering a wall at a university.
image.caption: Big-character posters at Peking University in 1967. Political writing became a public instrument of accusation and factional struggle during the Cultural Revolution.

cards.name: Reform and Opening
cards.description: In December 1978, a major Communist Party meeting marked a shift toward economic development. Changes to farming, business and overseas investment followed over several years. Different places tried different policies, and officials expanded some experiments while arguing over others.
cards.note: 1978 is a political turning point in an extended process. Individual reforms have different starting dates; this card does not treat market reform as political democratization.

sections.title: New choices in farming and business
sections.text: Household farming arrangements let families keep more of the returns from their work. Local businesses grew, and market prices played a larger role in parts of the economy. These changes affected the rewards people received for producing and selling goods. They developed while the Communist Party retained political control.

sections.title: Growth changes everyday life
sections.text: Investment and migration connected villages, coastal cities and overseas markets. People gained new opportunities to earn money and move for work. Access to jobs, housing and welfare remained uneven, so growth affected households differently. The year 1978 marks an important political turning point in a longer process. Individual reforms had their own starting dates and did not all take effect together.

sourceLabels.https://blogs.worldbank.org/en/eastasiap: World Bank · Forty years of reforms
sourceLabels.https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated: World Bank · China’s special economic zones

dateReview.note: December 1978 is the political turning point used here. Individual reforms began at different dates.

cards.significance: Reform changed the incentives through which people farmed, worked and traded. Greater room for household decisions, enterprise and overseas exchange helped raise production and living standards, while uneven opportunities created new inequalities and pressures. The change matters because it reshaped everyday life without replacing the ruling party. It was also a process of experiments, reversals and extensions over years. Treating 1978 as a starting point helps locate that process, but no single meeting created the economy that developed afterward.

significanceSources.label: World Bank · Forty years of China’s reforms

image.alt: A large roadside sign reading Time is Money, Efficiency is Life.
image.caption: The reform-era slogan at Shekou in Shenzhen, photographed in 2017. It commemorates a shift in public economic language; it is not a photograph of the 1978 leadership meeting.

cards.name: Xuanwu Gate (玄武门) coup
cards.description: Li Shimin (李世民)’s path to the throne passed through an ambush in 626. His followers killed Crown Prince Li Jiancheng (李建成) and their brother Li Yuanji (李元吉) at the palace’s northern gate. Their father later abdicated, and Li Shimin (李世民) became Emperor Taizong (唐太宗).

sections.title: Securing the throne and its story
sections.text: The killings left Taizong (唐太宗) with a difficult claim to justify. His court brought collaborative historical writing into the palace and gave him a larger role in accounts of the dynasty’s foundation. Control of the government also gave the victor influence over how the struggle would be remembered.

sections.title: The celebrated emperor
sections.text: Taizong (唐太宗) later acquired a reputation for good government. That achievement and the violent succession are both parts of his reign. The deaths of his brothers are well established, while accounts presenting his victory as inevitable or entirely justified need more caution. Later readers inherited a story shaped partly by the court that benefited from the coup.

dateReview.note: 626 is confirmed by the scholarly study of Chang He and the coup.

cards.significance: The coup places a violent struggle behind one of China's most admired models of rulership. Taizong (唐太宗)'s later reputation for listening to ministers did not erase the killing through which he secured succession. His court also influenced the record through which later readers understood those events. This makes the episode important in two connected ways: it changed who would govern Tang, and it demonstrates how successful rulers could shape historical memory to reconcile troubling origins with claims to legitimate and exemplary authority.

significanceSources.label: Isenbike Togan · Court historiography in early Tang

image.credit: Attributed to Yan Liben · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: A painted emperor with attendants in formal court dress.
image.caption: A representation of Emperor Taizong traditionally associated with Yan Liben. It belongs to the imperial portrait tradition, not an eyewitness scene of the Xuanwu Gate coup or a cabinet meeting.

cards.name: Xuanzang (玄奘)’s return
cards.description: Xuanzang (玄奘) returned to Chang’an (长安) in 645 carrying Buddhist manuscripts. He had begun his journey despite an imperial travel prohibition. The traveller who left without permission now received recognition at the imperial centre.

sections.title: The work of translation
sections.text: Bringing manuscripts home began another long task. Translators needed to compare texts, decide on meanings and work together with continuing institutional support. Xuanzang (玄奘) sought to resolve differences among the Buddhist writings already available in China. His account of the western regions also preserved knowledge of societies beyond Tang rule.

sections.title: Learning from beyond the empire
sections.text: Xuanzang (玄奘) studied Buddhist thought at Nalanda (那烂陀寺), a major monastery and centre of learning in India, before bringing texts back to China. Buddhism was already established in China before Xuanzang (玄奘) travelled. He helped transform that existing tradition by bringing new texts and expertise into it. Chang’an (长安)’s intellectual life depended partly on knowledge acquired elsewhere and made accessible through collective work. Later religious biographies emphasized his heroic journey, while the translation enterprise required many people after he arrived home.

cards.note: Return: 645 CE. Accounts differ on his departure year; this marker does not depend on choosing between them.

dateReview.note: 645 is the return from the Indian pilgrimage, not the beginning of his translation career or journey.

cards.significance: Xuanzang (玄奘)'s return brought manuscripts and learning into translation projects that changed the resources available to Chinese Buddhists. The journey mattered because its results were studied, translated and debated, turning travel into lasting intellectual exchange. His account also preserved information about places beyond Tang's borders. The wider historical connection is the active work through which Chinese religious culture absorbed and transformed ideas from elsewhere. It took travellers, patrons and teams of scholars, rather than the movement of objects alone, to make that exchange influential.

significanceSources.label: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy · Xuanzang

image.credit: Artist or photographer unidentified · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: A painted travelling monk carrying a large bundle on his back.
image.caption: A fourteenth-century Japanese image of Xuanzang. The travelling monk is remembered through a later devotional portrait, not an eyewitness likeness.

cards.name: Battle of Talas
cards.description: In 751, Tang forces were defeated by an Abbasid army at Talas in Central Asia. The defeat showed the difficulty of projecting military power far from the imperial court. It did not end contact between the two worlds.

sections.title: Contacts after the fighting
sections.text: Abbasid embassies continued to visit the Tang court after the battle. Du Huan (杜环), taken captive, eventually returned by merchant ship with observations of life abroad. Diplomats and merchants could keep moving even while armies fought. Military rivalry and exchange were part of the same connected region.

sections.title: Did captives spread papermaking?
sections.text: A famous story credits captured Chinese papermakers with bringing the craft to the Islamic world. The details remain disputed. Paper was already used in Central Asia before 751, and the battle’s exact role in spreading production is uncertain. Talas cannot securely be treated as the single moment that transferred the technology or instantly transformed the region’s religion.

cards.note: 751 CE. The papermaking narrative is disputed; the battle did not instantly Islamize Central Asia.

dateReview.note: 751 is confirmed. The existing note correctly distinguishes the battle date from the disputed paper-transmission story.

cards.significance: Talas reveals the limits of Tang military reach and the competing powers shaping Central Asia. It should not be made to carry every later change in the region: Chinese influence, trade and the movement of technologies followed different paths, and the familiar story tying papermaking's spread to this single battle is uncertain. Its value in the larger history is to place Tang within a political world it could influence without controlling completely. Military defeat and continuing cultural exchange could exist together.

significanceSources.label: Encyclopaedia Iranica · Chinese connections
Encyclopaedia Iranica · Paper and Papermaking

image.alt: A river winding through a green valley beneath mountains.
image.caption: A modern view of the Talas River. The landscape locates the region of the 751 encounter without identifying the exact battlefield or reconstructing its armies.

cards.name: Two-Tax reform
cards.description: In 780, Yang Yan (杨炎) proposed taxing households where they actually lived and grading their payments by wealth. Collection took place in summer and autumn. The government was trying to raise income from a population that no longer fitted its older records.

sections.title: Finding people and property to tax
sections.text: The proposal covered settled farmers and travelling merchants. Instead of relying only on inherited household categories, officials would assess the property and activity they could identify. This changed both how the court collected money and the basis on which households owed it.

sections.title: Who carried the burden?
sections.text: The official Lu Zhi (陆贽) warned that the reform made emergency wartime demands permanent. He also argued that farming property was easy to find while mobile wealth could escape assessment. A more adaptable system was therefore not necessarily fairer. The name Two Taxes refers to the two collection seasons, rather than simply to two kinds of taxable goods.

cards.note: 780 CE. Surviving memorials record both Yang Yan (杨炎)’s proposal and Lu Zhi (陆贽)’s criticism.

dateReview.note: 780 is the promulgation year of the Two-Tax system.

cards.significance: The reform adjusted taxation to a society that no longer fitted older assumptions about registered households and allotted land. That helped the Tang court seek dependable income after war had disrupted its authority and records. The change connects a military crisis to a longer transformation in the relationship between government and economic resources. It also explains why tax reform provoked moral argument: making revenue collection more practical for officials did not automatically make demands lighter or fairer for the people paying them.

significanceSources.label: Columbia University · Asia for Educators

image.credit: Gary Lee Todd, Ph.D. · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: A group of bronze cash coins with square holes.
image.caption: Tang Kaiyuan tongbao coins. The currency type began in 621, before the Kaiyuan reign period; the coins supply contemporary monetary context for Tang taxation without representing an actual Two Tax payment.

cards.name: Huichang (会昌) suppression of Buddhism
cards.description: In 845, Emperor Wuzong (唐武宗) ordered a major suppression of Buddhism. Clergy were forced back into lay life, and the state took control of monastic resources. Other religious communities were also targeted.

sections.title: Religion, labour and property
sections.text: Wuzong (唐武宗)’s edict accused religious institutions of consuming wealth and labour while avoiding duties to families and the ruler. Taking their property and returning clergy to ordinary registration would redirect resources toward the state. Religious hostility and the emperor’s Daoist commitments worked alongside these material interests.

sections.title: A deeply rooted tradition
sections.text: The court described Buddhism as foreign, although it had long been embedded in Tang society. That accusation helped justify persecution; it did not describe the loyalties of every believer. Official reports of destruction also came from the government carrying it out, so their totals cannot be treated as independently verified counts.

cards.note: 845 marks the major suppression, following earlier restrictions. Transmitted totals for clergy affected conflict.

dateReview.note: 845 marks the major suppression; broader restrictions and consequences extend beyond this point.

cards.significance: The suppression exposed a central tension in imperial government: religious communities could command land, labour and loyalty that rulers wanted to regulate or reclaim. Wuzong (唐武宗)'s attack disrupted Buddhist institutions, yet Buddhism remained deeply rooted in Chinese society and survived changes in imperial favour. The larger significance is the uneven relationship between state power and religious life. Court support could help institutions grow, but it also made their privileges vulnerable when a ruler redefined them as a financial burden or political threat.

significanceSources.label: Columbia University · Asia for Educators

image.credit: Anonymous Tang printers; commissioned by Wang Jie · British Library
image.alt: A printed Buddhist assembly above columns of Chinese text.
image.caption: The frontispiece of the Diamond Sutra dated 868, now in the British Library. Its survival makes the relationship between devotion, sponsorship, and woodblock reproduction unusually concrete. This Buddhist print dates to 868, after the 845 persecution, and is shown as evidence of the religious activity that continued after the suppression.

cards.name: Huang Chao (黄巢)’s occupation of Chang’an (长安)
cards.description: Huang Chao (黄巢)’s forces entered Chang’an (长安) at the beginning of 881. Their occupation, interrupted by renewed fighting, continued until 883. War damaged the farming that supplied the city, and famine added to the suffering caused by violence.

sections.title: Holding a capital
sections.text: Possession of Chang’an (长安) gave Huang Chao (黄巢) a powerful symbol of imperial authority. Keeping a government alive required more: food for inhabitants, control of the surrounding countryside and dependable military support. Capturing the palace did not automatically provide these things.

sections.title: A city damaged by war
sections.text: The destruction reached beyond court politics into the livelihoods that sustained urban life. Tang survived until 907, so people living through the occupation did not yet know its eventual dynastic outcome. Chang’an (长安)’s immediate crisis was one of fighting, disrupted supplies and hunger, as well as a struggle over who would rule.

cards.note: Use 881 CE. Accounts assigning the capture to 880 often follow the twelfth lunar month of the first Guangming regnal year.

dateReview.note: 881 CE is correct for the January capture; 880 in regnal/lunar chronology should not replace the Common Era year.

cards.significance: The occupation weakened an imperial centre whose authority depended on supplies and military cooperation beyond its walls. Holding Chang'an (长安) could make a powerful claim to rulership, but hunger and disrupted production exposed the difference between taking a capital and governing its supporting region. The conflict also belongs to the rise of commanders who would reshape late Tang politics. Its importance lies in those damaged relationships and shifting resources, rather than in treating the city's fall as the moment Tang immediately ceased to exist.

significanceSources.label: Cambridge History of China and historical research

cards.pinyin: huáng cháo gōng rù cháng ān

image.credit: Artist or photographer unidentified · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: A woodblock portrait of a bearded man in formal robes.
image.caption: A seventeenth-century illustration of Huang Chao from a historical narrative. It belongs to the rebel’s later reputation and must not be mistaken for a contemporary portrait.

cards.name: Tang’s fall and Later Liang’s foundation
cards.description: Zhu Wen (朱温) established Later Liang in 907, ending Tang and beginning the northern Five Dynasties sequence. He had previously fought in Huang Chao (黄巢)’s rebellion and then become a Tang military commander.

sections.title: From rebel to emperor
sections.text: Zhu Wen (朱温) carried military power through several changes of allegiance. The troops and connections that supported an imperial servant could later support a claimant to the throne. Tang’s formal end confirmed a shift toward regional commanders that had already been developing.

sections.title: Different regional experiences
sections.text: Northern dynasties changed frequently, while some southern kingdoms lasted longer and supported considerable prosperity. Tang’s fall therefore did not produce the same conditions everywhere. The Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms were overlapping governments in different regions, rather than fifteen rulers succeeding one another over a single united territory.

cards.note: 907 CE. The date is a dynastic transition, not the disappearance of every Tang institution or cultural practice.

dateReview.note: 907 is the dynastic transition to Later Liang.

searchAliases: Tang gives way to Later Liang
Tang’s fall and Later Liang’s foundation
cards.significance: Tang's formal fall gave a dynastic name to a transfer of power already developing through provincial armies. It opened a period in which northern commanders repeatedly claimed the throne while regional courts maintained separate governments. This connects the late Tang military order to the problems Song would later try to solve. The year is a useful boundary, but the deeper change was how authority depended on armed coalitions and regional resources that no single imperial title could instantly bring under control.

significanceSources.label: Cambridge History of China and historical research

image.credit: Artist or photographer unidentified · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: Women gathered inside a palace in a vertical painting.
image.caption: Palace Banquet, a painting assigned to the tenth-century Five Dynasties–early Song milieu, in the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Court culture continued across rapid political changes. The painting belongs to the period after Tang authority dissolved, not to the abdication of 907 itself.

cards.name: Laozi (老子) and the Daodejing (道德经)
cards.description: Laozi (老子), the “Old Master,” is associated with the Daodejing (道德经), a short book central to later Daoist traditions. His identity and lifetime are uncertain. The approximate Warring States dates here concern the book’s formation, rather than a securely documented person’s lifespan.

sections.title: The value of restraint
sections.text: The text questions forceful ambition, excessive desire and rulers’ confidence that they can impose order. Its idea of wuwei, often translated as non-action, does not simply mean doing nothing. It asks how action might avoid needless interference and ambitions that defeat themselves. Readers disagree about exactly how this advice should guide either a person’s life or a government.

sections.title: A book in different forms
sections.text: Guodian (郭店) manuscripts preserve related passages by around 300 BCE. Copies found at Mawangdui (马王堆) arrange material differently from the familiar later text. The book developed through copying and compilation. The story of a sage writing it all at a frontier pass belongs to later tradition and cannot replace this evidence of different early versions.

cards.note: Ca. 400–250 BCE is an interpretive composition range with uncertain boundaries. Tradition places Laozi (老子) earlier; this card does not assert an invented birth year or a single author.

dateReview.note: 400–250 BCE is interpretive text-formation range, not Laozi lifespan. SEP describes fourth-century development and relatively stable form by mid-third century. Existing approx and caveat are appropriate.

searchAliases: Laozi and the making of the Daodejing
cards.significance: The Daodejing (道德经) supplied a lasting challenge to the belief that greater effort or tighter control always improves life. Its arguments about restraint could speak to rulers, religious practitioners and people seeking a different way to live. Commentaries and ritual use kept renewing that relevance across dynasties. The book helps explain why Chinese intellectual history contains powerful alternatives within its own traditions to ambition and coercion. Its continuing influence belongs to generations of interpretation, even though the identity of its earliest authors remains uncertain.

significanceSources.label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy · Laozi

image.alt: An elderly robed figure riding an ox in a hanging-scroll painting.
image.caption: Zhang Lu’s Ming-period painting of Laozi riding an ox. This much later image belongs to the philosopher’s cultural afterlife; it cannot establish what the historical author looked like.

cards.name: Mozi (墨子)
cards.description: Mozi (墨子) and his followers challenged aggressive war, luxury and inherited privilege during the Warring States era. He probably taught in the later fifth century BCE, though his exact dates are unknown. The surviving book Mozi (墨子) includes arguments developed by followers as well as teachings associated with the master.

sections.title: Care beyond the family
sections.text: Mohists argued that concern for people should extend beyond family and political borders. Judged by the suffering it caused, aggressive war was hard to defend, whatever glory a ruler claimed. They also criticized lavish funerals and musical displays. Labour and resources, they argued, should benefit people broadly rather than mainly enhance the standing of the powerful.

sections.title: Order and capable officials
sections.text: This wider care went together with support for hierarchy, common moral standards and the promotion of capable officials. Mohists appealed to Heaven and spirits while also arguing carefully about practical consequences. Their ideas do not fit neatly into a modern political party. They pressed opponents to explain whose welfare deserved attention and which uses of resources could be justified.

cards.note: Around 430 BCE marks Mozi (墨子)’s approximate period of activity, not his birth or death. His precise dates are unknown.

dateReview.note: 450–390 BCE was editorial movement window, not a directly evidenced life interval. Prefer explicitly supported fl. c. 430 BCE marker. Existing description of later fifth-century activity remains valid.

cards.significance: Mohist arguments show that early Chinese thought included organized criticism of warfare and elite expenditure on the grounds of their consequences for ordinary people. This challenged rulers and rival teachers to explain whose interests their preferred customs served. Mohism did not become the dominant imperial teaching, but its surviving arguments preserve alternatives that a simple story of Confucian continuity would miss. Its place in the larger history is to widen the debate: hierarchy, public welfare and moral judgment could be combined in more than one way.

significanceSources.label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy · Mohism

image.alt: A printed page with vertical columns of Chinese characters.
image.caption: A page from an edition of the Mozi. The transmitted text gives access to Mohist arguments; this later printed page is not a manuscript from Mozi’s lifetime.

cards.name: Mencius (孟子)
cards.description: In the fourth century BCE, Mencius (孟子) developed teachings about moral growth and humane government. Dialogues with rulers in the book bearing his name connect a ruler’s authority with his treatment of people. Followers and later editors transmitted the text, and his conventional life dates remain approximate.

sections.title: People needed secure livelihoods
sections.text: Mencius (孟子)’s claim that human nature is good concerns capacities that need to be developed. It does not mean everyone always behaves well. He connected conduct with living conditions: a ruler who leaves people insecure and then punishes their misconduct cannot blame character alone. Providing for people and helping them learn were parts of the same responsibility.

sections.title: A throne did not settle the question
sections.text: The text permits harsh criticism of rulers who abandon their duties. It assumes monarchy and different social roles, rather than modern government by the people. Even so, holding the throne did not automatically make a ruler worthy of it. Later readers could use this argument to advise a ruler or condemn his failures.

cards.note: Ca. 370–290 BCE is a conventional approximate lifespan. The received Mencius (孟子) is a layered transmission; familiar anecdotes are philosophical presentations, not verbatim court minutes.

dateReview.note: c. 370–290 BCE supported by Columbia educational chronology. Alternatives such as 372–289 exist; retain approximate flag.

cards.significance: Mencius (孟子) strengthened the argument that a ruler’s authority should be judged by the lives people could lead under him. His account of moral growth tied personal conduct to education and material security, giving later scholars grounds to criticize destructive government. The text’s later place among the Four Books carried these questions into generations of study. Its influence therefore reached beyond advice to a few Warring States rulers. It became part of the intellectual equipment through which educated people discussed the obligations, and failures, of power.

significanceSources.label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy · Mencius

image.credit: Kanō Sansetsu · ColBase: Integrated Collections Database of the National Museums, Japan / Tokyo National Museum
image.alt: A robed scholar seated in a Japanese ink painting.
image.caption: Kanō Sansetsu’s 1632 portrait of Mencius. A Japanese interpretation made almost two millennia later, it illustrates the wider East Asian reception of Confucian learning.

cards.name: Zhuangzi (庄子)
cards.description: The Zhuangzi (庄子) uses stories, humour and unexpected viewpoints to question familiar judgments. Zhuang Zhou (庄周) probably lived in the later fourth century BCE, but other writers contributed to the surviving book. The approximate dates here describe its early development, rather than one established lifespan.

sections.title: Useful to whom?
sections.text: Its stories ask who decides what has value. A tree that a carpenter finds useless may survive because no one wants to cut it down for timber. What looks like a disadvantage from one position can look different from another. Tales of skill and transformation similarly invite readers to reconsider the purposes behind their judgments.

sections.title: Living under demanding rulers
sections.text: Doubts about ambition and public office had force in a world where rulers could demand service and punish failure. The text also explores action that is skilled and responsive, less restricted by fixed categories. Later readers have interpreted it in very different ways. A slogan such as “everything is relative” misses the variety and movement of its arguments.

cards.note: Ca. 350–250 BCE is an approximate setting for early composition and development. Authorship of individual chapters and the relation between the historical figure and the book remain debated.

dateReview.note: 350–250 BCE is a selected window for early textual development; SEP supports late-fourth-century author activity and subsequent layers, not these exact endpoints. Existing note explicitly identifies an approximate textual range. Preserve distinction from life dates.

searchAliases: Zhuangzi: perspectives and the art of living
cards.significance: The Zhuangzi (庄子) gave later readers ways to question the categories through which people judge success, usefulness and even their own knowledge. Its stories could loosen the hold of public status and invite other ways of valuing a life. Philosophers and writers returned to that freedom across very different political settings. This is important in the grand arc because Chinese culture developed through argument and imaginative challenges as well as official learning. A book could endure by unsettling familiar answers rather than providing a single governing programme.

significanceSources.label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy · Zhuangzi

image.alt: A seated Daoist figure in a painted scroll.
image.caption: A Yuan-period representation of Zhuangzi associated with Hua Zili. It is a later image of the thinker, not a contemporary portrait.

cards.name: Xunzi (荀子)
cards.description: Xunzi (荀子) defended learning, ritual and deliberate self-improvement in the third century BCE. He disagreed with Mencius (孟子) about the relationship between human nature and moral conduct. His dates are uncertain; he was still alive after his patron Lord Chunshen (春申君) was killed in 238 BCE.

sections.title: Learning to handle desire
sections.text: Unchecked desires could bring people into conflict over limited resources. Teachers and inherited practices helped people respond differently. Ritual organized expectations, emotions and distinctions between roles so that cooperation became possible. For Xunzi (荀子), good conduct was an achievement developed through practice, rather than simply the release of goodness already present within us.

sections.title: Human responsibility for government
sections.text: Xunzi (荀子) distinguished Heaven’s regular patterns from the success or failure of human rule. People had to take responsibility for the institutions they created. He valued disciplined effort, hierarchy and accomplished earlier teachers. Some later Confucian traditions gave him less prominence, but his disagreements show how widely early thinkers could differ while working with Confucius (孔子)’s inheritance.

cards.note: About 310 BCE is an estimated birth date. 238 BCE marks his latest securely documented activity, not a known death year. His description of human nature depends on a distinction between natural desires and learned moral conduct.

dateReview.note: c. 310 BCE birth estimate and alive after 238 BCE are supported. Existing note correctly says 238 is not death; date display should say c. 310–after 238 BCE, not merely 310–238.

searchAliases: Xunzi: learning makes an ethical world
cards.significance: Xunzi (荀子) made deliberate learning and shared practices central to explaining how people could live together. His disagreement with Mencius (孟子) shows that Confucian thought was never one settled account of human nature. By emphasizing the work needed to cultivate conduct, he gave ritual and institutions a practical role in forming society. Later preferences for Mencius (孟子) sometimes obscured that alternative. Reading Xunzi (荀子) restores an important strand of Chinese debate about whether good order depends chiefly on developing moral potential, reshaping habits or designing effective institutions.

significanceSources.label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy · Xunzi

image.credit: 国立国会図書館 · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: Facing pages of an old printed Chinese philosophical text.
image.caption: An Edo-period Japanese edition of the Xunzi, around 1745, from the National Diet Library. The printed book shows the later East Asian transmission of a Warring States text.

cards.name: Han Fei (韩非)
cards.description: Han Fei (韩非), who died in 233 BCE, examined how rulers could control ministers and subjects. The Han Feizi (韩非子) discusses standards, rewards, punishments and methods of government. Later writers called him a Legalist, though this label groups thinkers who did not form one organized school.

sections.title: Officials had interests of their own
sections.text: A minister might hide information, exaggerate success or turn delegated duties into personal power. Han Fei (韩非) wanted ways to compare an official’s performance with his stated responsibilities. Government should work through repeatable arrangements instead of depending on unusually wise rulers and perfectly loyal servants.

sections.title: Rules in the ruler’s hands
sections.text: Common standards could weaken inherited exemptions, but their purpose was stronger royal control, rather than equal political rights. The ruler kept command of rewards and punishments. This created a difficult dependence: he needed capable officials while fearing the independence their ability might give them. Han Fei (韩非)’s writing explores tensions inside powerful government, not a modern system of constitutional limits.

cards.note: About 280 BCE is a conventional approximate birth date; 233 BCE is his death year. The surviving collection has disputed layers. Legalism is a later classification, not modern rule of law.

dateReview.note: c. 280–233 BCE supported by University of Tuebingen authority record; birth approximate, 233 death. Current note correctly distinguishes them.

searchAliases: Han Fei: standards, incentives and distrust
cards.significance: Han Fei (韩非) focused attention on a ruler’s dependence on ministers who possessed knowledge and interests of their own. Standards, scrutiny and controlled rewards offered ways to address that problem without relying on everyone’s virtue. His arguments help explain the administrative side of imperial power alongside its moral language. They also expose a lasting tension: methods that protect the ruler can increase the control exercised over officials and subjects. Studying this tradition makes the machinery of government visible behind idealized portraits of wise emperors.

significanceSources.label: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy · Chinese philosophy and Han Fei

image.alt: A modern outdoor stone statue of a robed scholar.
image.caption: A modern statue of Han Fei in Shaanxi. The monument commemorates a thinker whose surviving arguments are textual; it does not preserve an ancient likeness.

cards.name: Mawangdui (马王堆) Manuscripts
cards.description: A tomb near Changsha (长沙), sealed in 168 BCE, preserved silk manuscripts with other burial materials. Excavations in 1972–1974 revealed the collection at Mawangdui (马王堆). The copies must be older than the tomb’s closure, but the works they contain may have been composed much earlier.

sections.title: What one collection held
sections.text: Philosophical writings appear alongside medical and technical materials and maps. The collection shows interests in government, health, the wider universe and bodily practices within one wealthy setting. It broadens our view beyond a few famous thinkers and books. It does not show a standard course of study followed by everyone in Han China.

sections.title: Different versions of a familiar book
sections.text: The Laozi (老子) manuscripts differ in wording and order from the later text. A book now encountered in a familiar form once circulated in alternatives. These copies help us see how texts changed as people transmitted them. A later edition’s authority does not mean that all earlier readers knew exactly the same words or arrangement.

cards.note: 168 BCE dates tomb 3’s closure. It is not a date for every Mawangdui (马王堆) tomb, every manuscript’s composition or the invention of the practices described.

dateReview.note: 168 BCE is evidenced by tomb 3 inventory slip; note correctly distinguishes burial/closure from composition. Scholarly manuscript record supports this specific dating.

searchAliases: Mawangdui: an archive beneath the earth
cards.significance: The Mawangdui (马王堆) manuscripts changed modern understanding of early Chinese learning by preserving texts outside the later history of copying and editing. Different versions of familiar works, alongside medical and practical writings, reveal a less neatly divided intellectual world. Their significance lies partly in allowing historians to compare what later tradition preserved with what an early Han household actually collected. The discovery makes the development of Chinese classics visible as a historical process, involving selection and variation rather than the unchanged transmission of finished books.

significanceSources.label: Princeton University · Methodology in the study of early Chinese manuscripts
Princeton University · The textual culture of the Mawangdui tombs

image.credit: Artist or photographer unidentified · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: Columns of Chinese text written on a damaged silk manuscript.
image.caption: A silk manuscript of the Laozi from Mawangdui, deposited in a Western Han tomb. The excavated text reveals a history of variation behind later standardized editions.

cards.name: Sima Qian (司马迁) and the Shiji (史记)
cards.description: Sima Qian (司马迁)’s Shiji (史记), or Records of the Grand Historian, brings together chronological accounts, tables, studies of government and society, and biographies. Written in the later second and early first centuries BCE, its 130 chapters include merchants, advisers and defeated rivals alongside emperors.

sections.title: More than one view of the past
sections.text: An emperor’s account can show a different world from a study of the economy or the life of someone he defeated. Readers have to connect these parts. The structure allows questions about behaviour, social position and how people gathered wealth and power, alongside the sequence of major events.

sections.title: History as criticism
sections.text: The economic chapters can be read as criticism of imperial expansion under Emperor Wu (汉武帝). That is an interpretation, rather than proof that every passage carries one hidden message. An official historian’s access to the court did not necessarily make him a simple spokesman for it. Writing about earlier events could also expose difficulties in the government of his own time.

cards.note: About 109–91 BCE is the usual composition range, not an exact publication schedule. Different portions and later transmission have their own histories.

dateReview.note: Existing c. 109–90 is rounded; 109–91 has direct source support. Neither is Sima Qian's lifespan; label already names composition.

searchAliases: Sima Qian and the Records of the Grand Historian
cards.significance: The Shiji (史记) helped establish how later Chinese histories would organize and judge the past. Its combination of chronology, institutions and individual lives allowed the story of empire to include defeated rivals and people outside the ruling house. Later historians adopted much of this form, making Sima Qian (司马迁)’s choices influential far beyond Han. The book matters both as evidence and as a way of thinking: it invites readers to compare reputation with conduct and to ask how individual decisions fit within larger political changes.

significanceSources.label: Library of Congress · Records of the Grand Historian
Cambridge University Press · Sima Qian’s critical past

image.alt: The opening page of an old printed Chinese historical text.
image.caption: An edition of the Shiji, the work associated with Sima Qian. A later printed witness to the text, rather than the author’s original manuscript.

cards.name: Salt and Iron Debate
cards.description: In 81 BCE, a court conference debated Emperor Wu (汉武帝)’s policies, including government monopolies on salt and iron. Huan Kuan (桓宽) later compiled the Discourses on Salt and Iron as an account of the exchanges. The debate asked what government should do and who should bear its costs.

sections.title: The price of frontier policy
sections.text: Supporters of government involvement in the economy argued that revenue paid for frontier commitments and public power. Critics pointed to hardship and the damaging effects of pursuing profit. Decisions about distant armies could affect the goods people produced and bought at home. Military policy and household burdens belonged to the same argument.

sections.title: A debate preserved by a later writer
sections.text: The speakers argued within a monarchy and a largely farming society. Modern labels such as capitalism and socialism do not neatly describe their positions. The surviving book also arranges arguments for later readers. It is evidence of political disagreement, but cannot recover every participant’s exact words or the full range of official opinion.

cards.note: 81 BCE dates the conference. The received text was compiled later; its speeches should not be treated as verbatim minutes or the complete views of all Han officials.

dateReview.note: 81 BCE conference supported by Columbia and Library of Congress; compilation occurred later, as card says.

searchAliases: The debate on salt and iron
cards.significance: The debate makes the costs of imperial strength visible. Frontier defence required revenue, while the ways officials raised it could burden the very households government claimed to protect. Both sides argued about public responsibility, making this more than a simple choice between a market and a state. Its longer significance lies in the recurring question it expresses: how far should rulers intervene in economic life, and who bears the consequences? The surviving text preserves disagreement within Han government rather than a single accepted imperial policy.

significanceSources.label: Columbia University · Debate on Salt and Iron

image.credit: Gary Todd from Xinzheng, China · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: A group of bronze Han cash coins with square holes.
image.caption: Western Han wuzhu coins associated with the official minting system established under Emperor Wu. They give material context to debates over state revenue and monopolies, not a depiction of the 81 BCE debate itself.

cards.name: Ban Zhao (班昭)
cards.description: Ban Zhao (班昭) helped finish the Book of Han after her brother Ban Gu (班固) died in 92 CE, and taught at the imperial court. Her Admonitions for Women became widely read. Her career shows a woman exercising authority through learning within a society that restricted women’s roles.

sections.title: Why should girls be taught?
sections.text: Ban Zhao (班昭) questioned giving education to boys while neglecting girls. She based her argument on women’s duties in marriage and ritual life, rather than calling for that social order to be abolished. Her writing could support learning for women while also expecting their subordination. Both parts matter to understanding what she argued.

sections.title: Advice and everyday life
sections.text: Rules about how women ought to behave cannot show that every household followed them. The text reflects expectations in a particular wealthy setting; its later readers gave it a wider influence. Ban Zhao (班昭)’s own achievement also warns against treating ancient women as one identical group. Access to education and court relationships could differ greatly.

cards.note: 92–ca. 116 CE marks her later scholarly career, not a precisely dated composition interval. Her birth is variously dated 45 or 49 CE; her death is approximate.

dateReview.note: 92–c. 116 CE is a selected late-career interval, bounded by Ban Gu death and Ban Zhao approximate death. It is not her lifespan or precisely dated composition range; existing note is correct.

searchAliases: Ban Zhao: scholarship and women’s education
cards.significance: Ban Zhao (班昭)’s career makes women’s participation in learned culture visible without hiding the restrictions they faced. Her historical work placed her within the production of authoritative knowledge, while her advice to women helped transmit expectations about family conduct. The combination complicates an easy story of either exclusion or liberation. Her later influence shows how education could give a woman a public voice while also being used to explain unequal duties. Understanding that tension helps connect the history of elite learning with the history of everyday social roles.

significanceSources.label: Columbia University · Ban Zhao, Admonitions for Women

image.alt: A painted scholar in long robes, holding writing materials.
image.caption: Gai Qi’s 1799 representation of Ban Zhao. This Qing image celebrates a Han woman of letters while also revealing the much later visual tradition through which she was remembered.

cards.name: Zhang Heng (张衡)’s earthquake detector
cards.description: In 132 CE, Zhang Heng (张衡) presented an instrument intended to indicate the direction of a distant earthquake. He also worked in astronomy, mathematics and literature. Observing natural events mattered at court because they could carry practical and political meaning.

sections.title: News of distant disaster
sections.text: An earthquake might damage a region far from the capital. It could also be interpreted as a warning about government. A device registering an event that people nearby had not felt offered a way to learn about the wider realm. Technical observation and beliefs about nature therefore worked together in this setting.

sections.title: What the device could do
sections.text: No original instrument survives. Modern reconstructions rely on descriptions that leave its mechanism uncertain. It was reportedly a detector of an earthquake and its direction, rather than an instrument drawing a continuous record or calculating magnitude. It did not predict earthquakes. These limits matter when judging the achievement: a modern reconstruction cannot establish every detail of how the Han device worked.

cards.note: 132 CE is the traditional presentation date. The original mechanism and the precision of reported performance remain debated; modern reconstructions are not surviving Han machines.

dateReview.note: 132 CE device date supported by St Andrews. Existing caution about mechanism and reconstructions appropriate.

searchAliases: Zhang Heng and the earthquake detector
cards.significance: Zhang Heng (张衡)’s work connects technical observation with the responsibilities of imperial government. An earthquake could indicate a distant disaster and also raise questions about the ruler’s conduct, giving the court reasons to seek better information. His instrument belongs to this wider effort to make events beyond immediate human perception observable. Its importance does not require treating modern reconstructions as surviving ancient machines. The historical record reveals an ambitious relationship between learning, devices and public authority, even where the instrument’s exact working cannot be recovered securely.

significanceSources.label: University of St Andrews · Zhang Heng

image.credit: Gary L. Todd, Ph.D., Professor of History, Sias International University, Xinzheng, China · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: A pottery model of a multi-storey palace building.
image.caption: A Han pottery architectural model. Such burial objects offer evidence for an elite built environment; they are contextual material, not a reconstruction of Zhang Heng’s instruments.

cards.name: Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art
cards.description: The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art collects problems about land areas, quantities, distribution, engineering and calculation. It developed over generations. Later explanations, especially Liu Hui (刘徽)’s commentary in 263 CE, became part of how readers learned from it.

sections.title: Methods for new problems
sections.text: Surveying a field or dividing resources required more than one numerical answer. A procedure could be used again with different quantities, helping learners solve new problems. The book connects general mathematical reasoning to situations familiar to officials and producers. Its practical settings do not make its methods merely mechanical.

sections.title: Learning through explanation
sections.text: The problems, operations and later commentaries worked together. Comparing their organization only with Greek geometry can overlook the reasoning expressed in a different form. Understanding the book requires attention to how its procedures were explained and taught. Its changing layers also make a single publication date misleading: the collection and the explanations added to it belong to different times.

cards.note: About 100 BCE–100 CE is a broad Han-period reference, not an established formation range. Proposed origins include around 200 BCE and alternative dating between 100 BCE and 50 CE. Different layers have different dates; Liu Hui (刘徽)’s commentary dates to 263 CE.
